#6094. Delta Air Lines Set To Reveal New 17-Hour Nonstop Route Next Week: See Map Now

Delta Air Lines has fallen behind United Airlines in terms of its transpacific network in recent years, but the Atlanta-based carrier has started to close that gap. This year, it reinstated flights between Los Angeles and Hong Kong, and next year it is reinstating its nonstop services between Seattle and Tokyo Narita, and also launching flights to Manila.

The airline is now preparing to announce yet another addition to its network next week. The SkyTeam member is hosting a major event in Seattle on December 2, where it is set to unveil at least one new route. It is widely expected to be Singapore, which it last served in 2019 via Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT).

Delta has been planning a return to the Lion City for some time. As Simple Flying reported in August, the airline's Chief Commercial Officer, Joe Esposito, confirmed that Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) was part of its future network plans. There has since been further evidence that the service could launch as early as next year.

Evidently, according to View From The Wing, the Atlanta-based airline identified Singapore as one of its new markets for 2027 in a July 29 presentation to a Pacific air traffic coordination group. The airline stated in the presentation, “New markets announced for 2027 are Manila and Singapore.”

The service is expected to operate from the airline's West Coast hub at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) and would have an estimated block time of around 17 hours. Delta will likely deploy its Airbus A350-900 on the route, although the larger A350-1000 could eventually take over the service.

Based on what is known so far, the service could launch in the summer or fall of 2027. Delta previously indicated that its Singapore service would follow the launch of its Los Angeles–Manila route. The latter is scheduled to commence on March 28, 2027, initially operating three times weekly before increasing to daily on June 7.

Singapore was once part of an extensive connecting network through Tokyo that Delta inherited from Northwest Airlines. When the carrier decided to withdraw from the Singapore market, it cited financial pressure on the route. Growing nonstop capacity between the US and Singapore, stronger brand loyalty towards local carriers, and competition from Star Alliance members at Changi made it increasingly difficult for Delta to compete.

But the proposed service would put Delta in direct competition with Singapore Airlines. According to scheduled data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, the Singaporean flag carrier operates five weekly flights between Seattle and Singapore. It also dominates the wider US–Singapore market, as noted above in the table. Meanwhile, United Airlines is currently the only US carrier serving Singapore nonstop, operating twice daily from San Francisco.

Only 2 airports in the Pacific are in Delta Air Lines' plans. Is this really enough, or is this actually a global trend in development?

It is interesting to see Delta expanding its presence in Asia. Its overall capacity in Asia is up around 5.8% this year compared to 2025. As noted earlier, there have been several interesting developments in its transpacific network. In June, the airline reinstated daily flights between its Southern California hub and Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) after decades of absence on the route.

Notably, it also marked its return to Hong Kong for the first time since 2018. From March 27, 2027, the airline will resume daily flights between Seattle and Tokyo Narita for the first time since March 2020, complementing its existing service to Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND). Elsewhere, it will make its debut in the Philippines market.

While not part of its regular network, the SkyTeam member has also scheduled a handful of nonstop flights to and from Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) for the upcoming Consumer Electronics Show (CES). These include flights between Las Vegas and Hong Kong on January 4 and 10, and between Las Vegas and Taipei on January 5 and 10.

#6093. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

As one of the world's largest cruise ships, Royal Caribbean's Legend of the Seas promises no shortage of things to see, do and eat. With an expansive lineup of dining and entertainment venues, pools and activities, there's enough onboard to fill an entire vacation without ever stepping off the ship.

But as someone without extensive cruising experience, I boarded the ship with a few preconceived notions about what the rooms, crowds and restaurants would be like.

After sailing on the ship's inaugural voyage, however, I found myself pleasantly surprised by several aspects of the experience. Here are five things I didn't expect.

With thousands of passengers on board, I expected finding a place to lounge by the pool, grab a drink or simply sit and relax to be a bit of a challenge. After all, even the largest cruise ship in the world has a finite amount of space.

Given that the ship's double-occupancy capacity is 5,610, I was surprised by how rarely I felt surrounded by crowds.

I was traveling with a friend, and we could almost always find available lounge chairs; we rarely encountered long lines at restaurants, bars or other public areas. Elevators were easy to navigate, and I never felt like I was constantly waiting behind a crowd of other passengers.

There were a few exceptions. Some of the pools got busy, and popular performances and events filled up quickly, so planning ahead was important if I wanted to see something specific. But even during popular moments, like the rooftop deck fireworks display, there was enough room to enjoy the show without feeling packed in.

The same was true during our visit to Perfect Day at CocoCay, Royal Caribbean's private island in the Bahamas. We spent time at South Beach and Cove Beach, where there were plenty of open spots to settle in and enjoy a peaceful vibe.

For a ship carrying so many passengers — up to 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity — I was surprised by how easy it was to find a little breathing room.

Related: The ultimate guide to Royal Caribbean cruise ships and itineraries

Cruise lines aren't shy about advertising their entertainment, but I wasn't entirely sure what to expect from the actual productions. I figured there would be plenty of activities to keep passengers occupied, but I didn't anticipate the caliber of performances I saw onboard.

The AquaTheater show was one of the highlights of my sailing. The production featured acrobatics, high dives and aerial stunts that had the audience audibly gasping throughout the show.

The ice skating production Fusion was another standout. The performers were incredibly talented, and the show was engaging from beginning to end. There was also a full production of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” that I unfortunately didn't have time to see.

Beyond the major productions, there was plenty of entertainment to stumble upon throughout the ship. The live music was consistently good, and we happened upon a silent disco where passengers of all ages were dancing while listening to music through their own headphones.

We also participated in an onboard escape room, which was just as thoughtfully designed and challenging as some of the escape rooms I've experienced on land.

I went into the sailing thinking of entertainment as something to do between meals and pool time. Instead, it became one of the reasons I was excited to explore the ship.

Related: The 7 classes of Royal Caribbean cruise ships, explained

I knew Legend of the Seas would have plenty of dining options, from casual restaurants to more upscale specialty dining. But I wasn't expecting one of my favorite experiences of the entire sailing to be an eight-course tasting menu at the Old Hollywood Supper Club.

The experience felt completely removed from the typical cruise-ship dining environment. The restaurant's glamorous old Hollywood decor, live musical quartet and immersive atmosphere made dinner feel like an evening out in its own right.

The eight-course menu was thoughtfully presented, with each dish accompanied by a corresponding cocktail. Our servers were incredibly knowledgeable about the food and drinks, and there were little surprises throughout the meal, including an amuse-bouche to start and an unexpected dessert at the end.

Some highlights included blinis with caviar and goat cheese, which came paired with what the restaurant called a Sunset Martini, and the wagyu filet, which was paired with the club’s version of an Old Fashioned. Even the palate cleanser — a vodka-infused sorbet presented theatrically under a smoky glass top — was well thought out and delicious.

It was a three-hour dining experience with enough time to enjoy each course, discuss all the flavors with my tablemates, enjoy the live music (which included songs that coincided with each course) and get excited about what was coming next in the story. For a few hours, I almost forgot I was eating aboard a cruise ship.

I assumed this ship would have plenty of casual, approachable, kid-friendly dining options (which it did), but this experience made me realize there are also opportunities for a more sophisticated night out onboard.

With so many restaurants, bars, pools, entertainment venues and distinct neighborhoods, I assumed it would take me a while to get my bearings on Legend of the Seas. But the ship's size never felt overwhelming, and I found it surprisingly easy to navigate. Clear signage made it simple to find my way between venues, elevator displays helped me figure out where I needed to go, and crew members were always nearby if I had a question.

That ease extended beyond the ship itself. The Wi-Fi connection was strong enough that I could research the different beaches and amenities at Perfect Day at CocoCay before we arrived, making it easy to plan how I wanted to spend my day. Once ashore, complimentary trams made it simple to get between different areas of the island without having to walk everywhere.

For a ship with so much happening at once, I appreciated how little effort it took to get where I wanted to go and make the most of my time.

Related: The best Royal Caribbean cruise ship for every type of traveler

Before this sailing, I had always pictured cruise ship cabins as fairly cramped spaces with just enough room for a bed and a small bathroom. I expected to spend most of my time out exploring the ship and very little time actually enjoying my room.

My cabin on Legend of the Seas changed that perception.

I stayed in a Spacious Infinite Ocean View Balcony Room, which had a large bed, a couch and a sitting area by the floor-to-ceiling window. There wasn't a true balcony, but the sitting area and full floor-to-ceiling window gave a balcony-like feel. Guests in these rooms can open and close the windows using a button on the side of the window.

There was a surprising amount of storage available in the room. Between the full closet, dresser drawers and bathroom shelves, there was plenty of room to unpack and keep everything organized rather than living out of a suitcase. There was also enough space for two people to get ready without constantly maneuvering around each other.

Of course, a cruise ship cabin isn't going to offer the same square footage as a traditional hotel room. But I was impressed by how thoughtfully the space was laid out and how comfortable it felt for two people.

Canada's second-largest airline will quietly pull out of Tulum. The airport, which serves the Southern Riviera Maya, will lose another airline despite strong travelers' interest in the region. Many carriers have scaled back operations at the airport, focusing instead on the region's primary gateway, Cancun. United Airlines was the latest major airline to announce it would terminate operations at the airport.

WestJet's withdrawal from Tulum will leave just two other Canadian airlines serving the airport, with Air Canada maintaining flights from Montreal and Toronto while Air Transat continues serving Tulum from Montreal and Quebec City.

On January 9, Montreal will lose its WestJet link to Tulum, as the airline terminates its Boeing 737 MAX 8 service to the Mexican airport. WestJet currently operates the route up to three times a week, with the link being operated for the carrier's package holiday subsidiary, Sunwing Vacations.

Mexico in general, and especially Cancun and the Riviera Maya, continues to be a popular year-round destination for Canadians looking for vacations to the south. WestJet's decision to drop its services to Tulum raises questions about the route's load factors, as the airline abruptly stopped flying there in the middle of the Canadian winter, usually a popular time to travel south.

With WestJet removing its flights from Montreal to Tulum, it leaves just Air Canada and Air Transat operating the service nonstop to Tulum. From Montreal to Cancun, Air Canada, Air Canada Rouge, Flair Airlines, Air Transat and WestJet all maintain services either seasonally or year-round.

Montréal-Pierre Elliott Trudeau International Airport (YUL)

Canada's largest city will also lose its WestJet link to Tulum, as on January 9 the carrier will axe its service to the Southern Riviera Maya airport. This will leave Air Canada as the sole operator on the city pair, making it yet another carrier unable to make operations at Tulum viable.

Instead, flights to and from the state of Quintana Roo will now be focused on Cancun, where WestJet maintains year-round flights. From Cancun, Toronto is served by Air Canada, Air Canada Rouge, Air Transat, Flair, Porter Airlines, and WestJet.

Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ)

WestJet, up until January served Tulum seasonally and has not maintained a year-round service. The same is true for Air Canada and Air Transat.

Three are long-haul, while the rest are within the Caribbean, Mexico and the US. Find them all here!

WestJet's home at Calgary is the third and final Tulum route the airline has cut. WestJet maintains a seasonal service to Tulum, flying up to twice weekly with a mix of the 737-800 and MAX 8. On January 14, the service to the Mexican tourist destination will be shelved, leaving no flights to Canada's west.

Despite Tulum continuing to be a world-class tourist destination, the local airport has struggled to gain momentum since its opening. WestJet joins a long list of airlines that have opted to withdraw service to the airport in recent months, most recently United Airlines, which will terminate its routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) on January 2 and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) on January 4. Domestic carrier Volaris will also end its nonstop flights to Tulum from Guadalajara on January 7.

Remaining airlines serving Tulum after January will be Air Canada and Air Transat from Canada, and American Airlines and Delta Air Lines with services to the US, as well as Mexicana de Aviación and Viva with domestic services within Mexico.

#6089. FAA Bans Line Up And Wait Operations “Forever,” With Even More Delays Expected

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has introduced stricter requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations at airports across the United States, effective November 24, 2026. The new rules require a dedicated air traffic control supervisor to oversee these operations, potentially preventing controllers at understaffed facilities from using the procedure. The change comes just as millions of Americans prepare to travel for Thanksgiving, raising concerns about longer departure queues and additional flight delays.

Despite reports describing the measure as a permanent nationwide ban, the FAA has not prohibited Line Up and Wait operations altogether. Instead, it has made them conditional on additional staffing, introducing another operational challenge for an air traffic control system already struggling with personnel shortages.

The new requirement is outlined in FAA Notice JO 7210.979, which mandates that a standalone watch supervision position must be staffed whenever Line Up and Wait operations are conducted. Previously, the relevant guidance recommended that the local control position should not be combined with other responsibilities. The updated wording makes this a mandatory requirement, meaning supervisors can no longer simultaneously perform other operational duties while overseeing these operations.

Line Up and Wait is a widely used air traffic control procedure that allows aircraft to enter an assigned runway and hold in position while waiting for takeoff clearance. It helps improve runway efficiency because departing aircraft are already positioned when the runway becomes available. However, under the new requirements, airports without sufficient personnel to provide dedicated supervision will have to keep aircraft waiting at taxiway holding points instead. This could reduce departure capacity, particularly during busy periods.

The timing is concerning because November 24 coincides with the beginning of one of America's busiest Thanksgiving travel periods. According to the FAA forecast reported by Traveling for Business, more than 52,000 flights were scheduled for that Tuesday, with over 417,000 expected throughout the nine-day holiday period.

FAA provided a statement to Simple Flying to clarify the new rule:

The FAA is taking proactive steps to further strengthen runway safety by enhancing staffing and supervisory requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) at airports nationwide, effective Nov. 24, 2026. These measures ensure dedicated controller staffing and supervisory oversight during LUAW operations and reinforce the FAA’s commitment to maintaining the highest safety standards. This will not impact airport operations.

Dedicated Local Control: The local control position responsible for arriving and departing aircraft must not be combined with any non-local control position.

Stand-Alone Watch Supervision: A dedicated watch supervision position must be staffed and cannot be combined with any other position. This strengthens existing guidance by making stand-alone watch supervision mandatory.

The controversy gained attention after a radio exchange at Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ). According to TheTravel, a controller told a Southwest Airlines crew about the new nationwide requirement, warning it could slow departures during the busiest travel time of the Thanksgiving rush. The controller described the restriction as something that would last forever, although the FAA's official notice did not use that wording.

Importantly, the FAA's stated objective is to improve runway safety, not reduce airport capacity. Having a dedicated supervisor overseeing operations should help prevent distractions and improve situational awareness when aircraft are positioned on active runways. The FAA's existing procedures also emphasize that Line Up and Wait is not takeoff clearance and that aircraft should not normally remain in that position for more than 90 seconds without further instructions.

But there is also an important clarification: the official notice lists June 9, 2027, as its cancellation date. Therefore, describing the measure as an indefinite or permanent prohibition is misleading. The actual impact will depend on staffing levels at individual towers and how frequently they can provide the additional supervisory position.

FAA ties delayed pay to efficiency metrics that demand more on position time amid a 3,000 controller shortfall.

The FAA is attempting to address its longstanding air traffic controller shortage through an ambitious recruitment campaign, including an unusual effort to attract video gamers. In October 2026, the agency announced that it had hired 2,235 controller trainees during the fiscal year, exceeding its recruitment target. The campaign reportedly attracted more than 12,000 qualified applicants within just 24 hours, demonstrating the potential of targeting candidates with strong multitasking and decision-making abilities.

However, recruiting additional candidates does not immediately solve the staffing problem. According to the FAA's 2026 workforce plan, becoming a fully certified controller can take more than two years, depending on the complexity of the assigned facility. The agency has set recruitment targets of 2,300 trainees for fiscal year 2027 and 2,400 for 2028, while expanding training capacity and modernizing its workforce management procedures.

As a result, the new Line Up and Wait requirements could create additional operational pressure before the benefits of increased recruitment become apparent. Although the measure is intended to strengthen runway safety, airports with limited staffing may have fewer opportunities to use an efficiency-enhancing procedure. For Thanksgiving travelers, the immediate concern is that an already busy aviation network could face additional departure bottlenecks during the holiday rush.

#6088. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6087. How The Airbus A350 Survives Environmental Stress During The Longest Flights In The World

Before entering commercial service, the Airbus A350 had to prove it could withstand some of the harshest conditions on Earth. Airbus needed to establish how its engines, systems, and structure would respond to extreme temperatures and demanding operating conditions. From the freezing Canadian Arctic to the scorching deserts of the United Arab Emirates and the high-altitude airports of Bolivia, Airbus deliberately pushed its new widebody aircraft to its limits.

Through these trials, Airbus sought to ensure that the A350 could operate safely and reliably across a wide range of environments. The A350 has since become a key aircraft for ultra-long-haul operations, including Singapore Airlines' nonstop flights between Singapore and New York. So, how did Airbus test the A350, and what did these trials reveal about the aircraft's capabilities?

Before entering commercial service, every new aircraft must undergo extensive testing and certification to demonstrate compliance with aviation safety standards. For Airbus aircraft, the main certification authority is the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), while the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) validates the design for the US market. The process begins with the Type Certificate (TC), which confirms that an aircraft's design meets the applicable airworthiness requirements. Manufacturers must also hold the relevant production approvals, while each individual aircraft requires a Certificate of Airworthiness (CoA) before entering service. Airlines must additionally meet operational requirements, including crew training, maintenance arrangements, and any necessary authorizations.

The certification process also varies depending on the aircraft's design and available configurations. For example, Airbus' A320neo Family certification program covered six airframe and engine combinations. The A319neo, A320neo and A321neo each required validation of their airframes, systems and two available engine options: the CFM International LEAP-1A and Pratt & Whitney Geared Turbofan (GTF). These campaigns also verified whether the aircraft met their performance targets for fuel consumption and range, reflecting improvements from the new engines and Sharklet wingtip devices.

For the A350-900, Airbus completed its flight-test and certification campaign in just over 14 months, setting an industry record for the program's completion time. Five test aircraft accumulated more than 2,600 flight hours, during which Airbus evaluated the aircraft's handling characteristics, systems, performance, and reliability. The campaign culminated in the A350-900 receiving Type Certification from EASA and the FAA in 2014. However, the program also involved specialized environmental testing in Canada, the United Arab Emirates, and Bolivia, along with controlled temperature trials at the McKinley Climatic Laboratory in the United States. These tests would establish how the A350 performed in conditions far beyond those encountered during routine airline operations.

In January 2014, Airbus took its A350-900 MSN3 development aircraft to Iqaluit, Canada, to conduct cold-weather trials in temperatures as low as -28°C. A team of 48 Airbus specialists assessed how the aircraft's engines and systems performed in freezing conditions. One key test involved starting the engines and auxiliary power unit (APU) after a cold soak, during which the aircraft was left exposed to extremely low temperatures for an extended period. The team also conducted system checks, low-speed taxiing, rejected takeoffs, and a local test flight to verify the aircraft's performance.

Three years later, Airbus returned to Iqaluit with the larger A350-1000, which underwent five days of intensive ground and flight testing in temperatures ranging from -28°C to -37°C. Alongside these Arctic trials, Airbus also used the McKinley Climatic Laboratory at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida, becoming the first Airbus aircraft to undergo testing at the facility. Unlike Iqaluit, where engineers depended on natural weather, the laboratory's climate-controlled hangar allowed Airbus to simulate temperatures from -40°C to +40°C under controlled conditions.

However, extreme cold was only one part of the A350's environmental testing program. While the Canadian trials focused on the aircraft's ability to operate in freezing conditions, Airbus also needed to assess its performance in extreme heat and at high-altitude airports. This took the A350 to Al Ain in the United Arab Emirates and La Paz in Bolivia, where high temperatures and reduced air density presented a different set of operational challenges.

Airbus has introduced new operational limitations affecting its narrowbody aircraft equipped with PW1100 engines.

While freezing temperatures presented one challenge, Airbus also needed to demonstrate that the A350 could operate safely in extreme heat. In July 2017, the manufacturer sent its A350-1000 test aircraft, MSN065, to Al Ain International Airport in the United Arab Emirates for a three-day hot-weather testing campaign. Conducted between 4 and 7 July, the trials exposed the aircraft to temperatures exceeding 40°C, reaching as high as 48°C. The objective was to assess how the aircraft's systems performed in scorching conditions, particularly the Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines and cabin air-conditioning systems.

One main concern was whether the aircraft could maintain comfortable cabin temperatures on the ground, where cooling systems must cope with intense external heat. Engineers also assessed engine performance, as higher temperatures reduce air density and affect engine thrust and takeoff performance. This can increase the runway distance required for departure, particularly at airports with shorter runways. The importance of these limitations became evident in June 2017, when extreme temperatures in Phoenix, Arizona, led to dozens of flight cancellations involving regional aircraft with lower maximum operating temperature limits.

According to Airbus, the A350-1000 successfully met all the parameters established for its Al Ain campaign, demonstrating its readiness to operate in extreme heat. However, high temperatures are not the only factor that reduces air density. Airports situated thousands of meters above sea level present similar performance challenges, even when outside temperatures are considerably lower. To assess these conditions, Airbus also conducted high-altitude testing in Bolivia.

Airbus also took the A350 to El Alto International Airport in La Paz, Bolivia, situated approximately 4,061 meters (13,325 feet) above sea level. At this elevation, air density is roughly 40% lower than at sea level under comparable standard conditions, creating significant challenges for aircraft performance. Thinner air reduces the amount of oxygen available to the engines, limiting the thrust they can produce, while also reducing the lift generated by the wings at a given airspeed. Consequently, aircraft generally require higher true airspeeds and longer take-off distances to become airborne.

High-altitude testing allows Airbus to evaluate how aircraft systems and engines respond to these demanding conditions. One particularly important assessment involves engine starting, which becomes more challenging as air density decreases. Engineers also examine thrust response, takeoff and climb performance, and the aircraft's handling characteristics. Jean-Philippe Cottet, Airbus' head of design development flight tests, identified starting engines at high altitude as one of the main reasons the manufacturer conducts trials specifically in La Paz.

The A350-900 and A350-1000 were among the aircraft Airbus tested at La Paz, which has also hosted other Airbus development programs. These evaluations help establish the aircraft's operational limitations and demonstrate its ability to perform safely at high-elevation airports. Together with the cold-weather trials in Canada and hot-weather testing in the UAE, the campaign provided evidence of the A350's capabilities across markedly different operating environments.

The Airbus A350 has a service ceiling of around 43,000 ft.

Beyond extreme weather testing, Airbus also needed to demonstrate how the A350 would perform during extended commercial operations. As part of its certification campaign, the manufacturer conducted a global route-proving program, visiting 14 major airports across four separate trips and covering approximately 81,700 nautical miles in 180 flight hours. Airbus also introduced an Early Long Flights (ELF) program, which went beyond regulatory certification requirements. These simulated commercial services carried Airbus employees acting as passengers, with airline flight crews operating a fully equipped cabin to evaluate onboard systems under realistic conditions. Such testing helped prepare the A350 for demanding long-haul operations, including Singapore Airlines' nonstop services between Singapore and New York, which use the A350-900ULR and can exceed 18 hours.

The A350's long-range capabilities are also central to Qantas' Project Sunrise, which aims to introduce nonstop flights from Sydney to London and New York using specially configured A350-1000ULR aircraft. Compared with the standard A350-1000, the Project Sunrise variant incorporates an additional fuel tank with approximately 5,283 gallons (20,000 liters) of capacity to support longer journeys. The A350's composite fuselage also resists corrosion and fatigue, while its cabin pressurization and environmental control systems allow a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet and higher humidity than many older aircraft. These features are particularly relevant on flights lasting 18 hours or more, where passenger comfort becomes increasingly important.

However, the ability to withstand extreme temperatures and remain airborne for extended periods is only part of the challenge. Ultra-long-haul operations also require careful management of crew fatigue, passenger wellbeing, maintenance schedules, and operational reliability. As airlines prepare to operate flights approaching 20 hours, the question is no longer simply how far an aircraft can fly, but rather how comfortably and efficiently passengers and crew can endure the journey.

While the A350's certification trials demonstrated its ability to withstand extreme operating conditions, flights approaching 20 hours present another challenge: passenger wellbeing. Ahead of its Project Sunrise services, Qantas partnered with researchers from the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre to investigate ways of reducing jet lag on ultra-long-haul flights. During experimental flights lasting approximately 20 hours, researchers monitored 23 volunteers wearing tracking devices as they followed specially designed schedules for meals, cabin lighting, sleep, and movement. Initial findings suggested that passengers following these routines experienced less severe self-reported jet lag, better sleep quality during the flight and improved cognitive performance in the two days following arrival compared with those following conventional inflight routines.

Qantas plans to incorporate these findings into its A350-1000ULR operations, including tailored cabin lighting, recommended meal and rest schedules, and a dedicated Wellbeing Zone where premium economy and economy passengers can stretch and move around. The airline also expects its nonstop Project Sunrise services to reduce total journey times by more than three hours compared with connecting flights. While Singapore Airlines' existing A350-900ULR operations have already demonstrated the aircraft family's suitability for ultra-long-haul services, Project Sunrise will provide another important test of its capabilities.

Ultimately, the success of these routes will depend not only on aircraft reliability and commercial performance, but also on how effectively airlines can make journeys approaching 20 hours comfortable for passengers and manageable for crews.

#6084. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

Schedule analysis using OAG data shows that all of the following markets saw the ULCC in Q1 2026 but will not do so in Q1 2027. Some may have had flights in January, February, and March this year, while others may have only had service in one or two of the months.

20 of them have been removed entirely from Allegiant's map due to what is normal route churn. No flights are planned beyond the stated month. The remaining six markets are very different. While they won't be served in the first three months of the new year, they'll simply return later in 2027. Some may say that including them is unfair, but they feature because two different time periods were compared.

#6081. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6079. Where To Spot The Air France Airbus A318 Before It Finally Retires

Air France's Airbus A318 was due to disappear from scheduled passenger service on November 8, but its retirement has been pushed back to March 27, 2027. The airline's remaining aircraft are still operating from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), with Marseille (MRS), Toulouse (TLS), Bordeaux (BOD), Nice (NCE), Milan Linate (LIN), and Lyon (LYS) offering some of the most frequent opportunities to catch the type.

Using data from the Simple Flying Flight Tracker, we analyzed 423 A318 flights between October 12 and November 8. The four aircraft visited 30 airports during those four weeks. One stopped appearing after October 20, although it has since returned to service. Their movements provide a useful indication of where and when to look, particularly for anyone planning a visit to Paris in the coming months.

The smallest member of the Airbus A320 family has already received several extensions to its service life with Air France. Last summer, the carrier extended planned A318 operations from November 8, 2026, until March 27, 2027. The revised timetable covers domestic French routes and a selection of intra-European destinations, with all the scheduled services operating through CDG.

However, March 27 is the final date currently shown in the published schedule rather than a confirmed farewell flight. Aircraft assignments can also change independently of the route timetable, meaning the presence of an A318 in a booking system does not guarantee that passengers will actually travel on one. For spotters, recent movements are consequently more useful than relying entirely on flights advertised several months ahead.

Air France has continued replacing its smaller A320-family aircraft with the Airbus A220-300. On November 6, the airline received its 60th A220, registered F-HOZJ, which subsequently entered passenger service on November 9. The new aircraft seats 148 passengers, compared with 131 on the A318, and is now used across much of the airline's European network. Nevertheless, the four remaining A318s continue to appear in daily operations.

The busiest A318 route during our four-week analysis was between CDG and Marseille Provence Airport (MRS), with 69 recorded flights in both directions. Of these, 35 departed Paris and 34 returned from Marseille. Toulouse-Blagnac Airport (TLS) came second with 47 flights, followed by Bordeaux–Mérignac Airport (BOD) with 42. Together, these three domestic connections accounted for 158 flights, or more than a third of the total activity recorded.

Nice Côte d'Azur Airport (NCE) was the fourth most frequently visited destination, with 28 flights. The leading international route was Milan Linate Airport (LIN), with 22, while Lyon–Saint Exupéry Airport (LYS) recorded 20. These six routes accounted for 228 of the 423 flights, making them the most useful starting points for anyone trying to photograph the aircraft away from CDG. The figures reflect actual recorded movements, not the number of A318 flights scheduled in the months ahead.

Marseille is particularly interesting because the A318 appeared on several different rotations rather than being restricted to a single flight number. AF7344 was recorded ten times from Paris during the analysis, while AF7336 appeared on eight departures. The late-evening AF7344 also operated with F-GUGP on November 21, according to subsequent flight history.

Airbus's whale-shaped jet keeps its operation moving across Europe and beyond.

Despite their small number, the A318s were used across a geographically diverse network. We identified 30 different airports in 12 countries between October 12 and November 8, including CDG itself. France accounted for nine of these airports, while the aircraft also visited five in Italy, four in Spain, and two in Portugal. Outside these markets, the tracking data included destinations such as Amsterdam (AMS), Copenhagen (CPH), Warsaw (WAW), Munich (MUC), Prague (PRG), and Bergen (BGO).

The aircraft were not limited to routes typically associated with the French domestic network. Recorded international flights include Paris to Casablanca Mohammed V International Airport (CMN), Málaga (AGP), and Ibiza Airport (IBZ). Bergen Airport (BGO) also appeared in the data, although each of these destinations was served far less frequently than the main domestic routes. A route appearing once or twice in four weeks should not be interpreted as a dependable spotting opportunity.

Unsurprisingly, of the 423 recorded flights, 422 either departed from or arrived at CDG. The exception was a one-off flight between Bologna (BLQ) and Venice (VCE) on November 6. The French hub airport therefore remains the most obvious location for seeing one without having to predict its next destination, although the timing of a visit makes a substantial difference.

This is the detour the world's longest Airbus A321XLR flight takes every day.

As each of the active A318s generally completes around five flights on a flying day, the aircraft make repeated appearances at CDG throughout the day. Our tracking data contains 213 departures from the airport during the 28-day period, equivalent to an average of approximately eight daily departures across the remaining fleet. These were not evenly distributed across the day, however, and several periods offered considerably more activity than others.

The most useful morning window was between 7:00 AM and 8:59 AM local time, when 49 A318 departures were recorded. Another 44 departures took place between noon and 1:59 PM, while 49 occurred between 6:00 PM and 9:59 PM. The later flights are less useful for photography during the winter months, although they provide additional opportunities for anyone primarily interested in watching or flying the aircraft.

Particularly at CDG, it is worth following the registration rather than concentrating on just one scheduled departure. An A318 arriving from Bordeaux, Marseille, or Milan may continue to an entirely different destination after its turnaround. Watching the aircraft's inbound sector can therefore help establish whether the same airframe is likely to operate the next flight, rather than waiting for a single flight number that may be assigned another type.

We tracked hundreds of flights in 2 weeks, revealing the busiest diversion airports, major disruption waves and 3 extraordinary detours in the world

Four registrations appear in the four-week dataset: F-GUGM, F-GUGN, F-GUGO, and F-GUGP. The busiest was F-GUGM, which completed 146 flights and was recorded on all 28 days. F-GUGO operated 129 flights across 26 days, while F-GUGN recorded 102 flights across 21 days after first appearing on October 19. On days when they flew, each aircraft generally operated around five sectors, although individual daily totals varied.

F-GUGP followed a different pattern as the aircraft completed 46 flights during the first nine days of the period, with its final recorded departure on October 20, when it flew from CDG to Casablanca. It did not appear again in our data through November 8. Consequently, the four-week figures primarily reflect the activity of three aircraft during the second half of the period, rather than a consistently deployed four-aircraft fleet.

More recent data shows F-GUGP operating AF7344 from CDG to Marseille on November 21, departing at 8:15 PM and landing at 9:21 PM. Its return to flying demonstrates why a list of active registrations needs to be checked against current movements, particularly as the retirement date approaches.

The A318's wider route network may contain many possible destinations, but the availability of the actual aircraft will determine which services operate as planned. With only four registrations to follow, a single aircraft being unavailable can affect a sizeable proportion of the type's daily flying. That is also why an A318 shown against a route weeks in advance is not necessarily the aircraft that will turn up on departure day.

The easiest way to identify an A318 currently flying is to open the Simple Flying Live Flight Tracker and search for the aircraft type or one of the four registrations. F-GUGM, F-GUGN, F-GUGO, and F-GUGP provide a much narrower starting point than following every Air France flight from Paris. Filtering the map around CDG then makes it possible to see which aircraft are airborne and where they are heading.

To find out where Air France's last A318s will fly, the most useful approach is to check the recent history of the individual aircraft and then compare it with the airline's upcoming flights. The four-week data suggests beginning with Marseille, Toulouse, and Bordeaux, before considering Nice, Milan Linate, or Lyon. However, the registration assigned on the day is more important than how often a particular route appears in October or early November.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

The tracker also allows you to follow the aircraft without traveling to France, while registration-level histories reveal patterns that published schedules miss. When the final A318 flights take place, the same historical data should provide the most reliable record of which aircraft operated the last passenger service, rather than relying on the timetable alone.

#6078. Capital One Venture Card Bonus: 75K Miles + $300 Credit Welcome Offer (Last Chance)

At the moment, the $95 annual fee Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is offering a phenomenal limited time welcome bonus, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d like to provide an update that this is the last chance to pick up the card with this offer, as it’s expected to be pulled soon.

Not only is this among the best offers we’ve seen on the card, but this is also a reasonably priced travel rewards card that offers long term value, especially for everyday spending.

Link: Learn more about the Capital One Venture Card

The Capital One Venture Card is currently offering a limited time, lucrative, two-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn 75,000 Capital One bonus miles, plus a $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, after spending $4,000 within the first three months.

For context, Capital One miles can be redeemed for a minimum of one cent each, meaning the 75,000 miles will get you at least $750 in value. However, I value the miles at 1.7 cents each based on my latest analysis (see my methodology here), thanks to the value you can get by transferring the miles to travel partners. That means that to me, the 75,000 miles are worth $1,275.

There are lots of great ways to redeem Capital One miles, as they can be transferred to Capital One’s roughly 20 airline and hotel partners. That’s my preferred use of them, as you can get some amazing travel experiences this way.

Partners include programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, and more. These are all programs that allow you to really maximize your points and get outsized value. Just to give a couple of examples of Capital One mileage redemption opportunities:

That doesn’t include the value of the $300 Capital One Travel credit, which posts upon account approval (rather than upon completing minimum spending). The idea is that this can be used for a hotel or vacation rental booking through Capital One Travel in your first cardmember year (in the first 12 months), and it’s valid across one or multiple stays. In other words, you could use it to pay virtually nothing for a $300 hotel stay. All-in-all, I’d say the Capital One Venture bonus is worth up to $1,575.

By my valuation, the current Capital One Venture Card bonus is the best publicly available offer that we’ve seen in over five years, so that makes this the ideal time to apply, and I absolutely wouldn’t wait for a better offer. Quite to the contrary, when this limited time offer gets pulled, it’ll almost certainly be worse.

For context, below is a history of the publicly available bonuses that we’ve seen on the Capital One Venture in recent years.

As you can see, we’ve never seen a publicly available welcome offer of over 75,000 miles, in terms of the mileage component. We have in the past seen $250 travel credits offered along with the miles, and this time around the travel credit is bigger. So offers really don’t get better than this on the card.

When you look at the bonus terms on the Capital One Venture Card, you’ll find the following language:

You are not eligible for this product if you have received a new cardmember bonus for the Capital One Venture card or the Capital One Venture X card in the past 48 months.

As you can see, the card follows a 48-month rule, so you’re not eligible for the welcome bonus on this card if you’ve received a new cardmember bonus on this exact card or on the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) in the past 48 months.

Other than that, eligibility is unrelated to having any other credit card, and Capital One doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for cards.

The Capital One Venture Card has a reasonable $95 annual fee, and offers a variety of perks beyond the excellent welcome bonus:

While the Capital One Venture Card is awesome, how does it compare to the Capital One Venture X Card, which is Capital One’s ultra premium credit card? The Venture X has a $395 annual fee, so the fee is significantly higher, but it also offers several great perks that should more than justify the annual fee. Among other things, the Venture X offers:

So when it comes to the Capital One Venture vs. Venture X, personally I think the Venture X is an even better value than the Venture. However, I know some people just want to avoid higher annual fee cards in general, so for those people, the Venture could be a better option.

The limited time Capital One Venture Card bonus currently offers 75,000 Capital One miles plus a $300 Capital One Travel credit upon completing minimum spending. This Capital One Venture bonus is significantly better than usual, so if you’re eligible for the card based on the 48-month bonus rule, I’d absolutely recommend applying. This is the last chance, as the offer is expected to be pulled soon.

Anyone plan to pick up the Capital One Venture Card with this great bonus?

#6077. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.

#6076. Delta Plans Seattle To Singapore A350 Flights, Carrier’s Third Longest Route

We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed plans to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional update, as an announcement about the new route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

Back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

My guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

One certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s new Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

In both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

It’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

It’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

The most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

Delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:

It also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

Delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a new Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

It’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time…

What do you make of Delta’s plans to fly to Singapore?
