#6074. Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Points With 80% Bonus (1.1 Cents Each): Worth It?

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is currently offering a best-ever promotion on purchased points. Through December 31, 2026, Flying Club members can purchase points with up to an 80% bonus, which is potentially an opportunity to buy points for under 1.1 cents each. Suffice it to say that this could be a very attractive deal.

Link: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus

Between 12AM GMT on November 24 and 11:59PM GMT on December 31, 2026, the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club program is offering a bonus on purchased points. Virgin Atlantic is offering a tiered bonus of up to 80%, as follows:

Note that the purchase of Virgin Atlantic points is non-refundable, and purchasing points doesn’t count toward Flying Club elite status. Points will be credited to accounts within 24 hours, though they typically post faster than that, and almost instantly.

The cost to purchase Virgin Atlantic points varies based on where your account is registered:

The pricing is much better for those with accounts registered in the UK rather than the US. Assuming you’re eligible for an 80% bonus:

So as you can see, in the United States you can potentially pay 1.39 cents per point, while in the UK you can potentially pay 1.09 cents per point.

It’s interesting how much Virgin Atlantic penalizes those in the United States when it comes to buying points. Then again, when it comes to overall points earning opportunities, we can’t really complain in the United States, given the amazing credit card offers we have.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club ordinarily lets members purchase up to 200,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been doubled, to 400,000 points.

When Virgin Atlantic Flying Club offers a promotion on purchased points, the best version of the offer is almost always for a 70% bonus. As you can tell, this offer is even better than those, as this is truly a best-ever offer. Personally, I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a short term use in mind, rather than based on the slight difference in the cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Flying Club program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Flying Club points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

Nowadays Virgin Atlantic has dynamic award pricing for its own flights, and for those with flexibility who want the best deal, this can make for some great deals. For example, there are some transatlantic one-way business class awards that cost under 30,000 points, which is amazing.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 52,500-60,000 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Flying Club points to be worth 1.1 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Flying Club points than that.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points don’t expire. There’s no requirement to even have any account activity, as the points will never expire regardless.

While buying Virgin Atlantic points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Flying Club points. Most significantly, Virgin Atlantic is partners with major transferable points currencies, including American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou, and in all cases, points can be moved at a 1:1 ratio. There are several ways to earn these points aside from outright buying them.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is offering members an 80% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for 1.09-1.39 cents each (in USD), depending on where your account is registered.

There are plenty of circumstances where this could be a great deal. The only major consideration is that there are lots of other ways to earn Virgin Atlantic points with transferable points currencies, so some may prefer to earn rewards that way. With a specific use in mind, there could definitely be huge value in buying Flying Club points.

Do you plan on buying Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus?

#6073. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6072. American Airlines Drops Its Chicago Gate Lawsuit—But United Isn’t Getting The Retreat It Wanted

American Airlines is dropping its lawsuit over Chicago O’Hare’s gate redistribution. The airline tells me it has filed to dismiss the underlying contract case after losing its injunction appeal — even as it continues to insist Chicago broke its lease. The airline has recovered gate space, added flights, and is in a much stronger position in Chicago than when the case began. American says two subsequent gate redeterminations have increased its allocation, and it also bought two gates from Spirit Airlines. They’re putting their attention into growing the hub, including a new Admirals Club that doubles the current L concourse lounge’s footprint. In a statement shared with me, American says: We stand by our decision to advocate for a fair process, and today, we believe the best way to continue delivering on that commitment is to look ahead. As rebuild our Chicago hub from the pandemic, we have continued to invest in our operation, network and customer experience. Our focus now is on continuing that momentum and building an even stronger future at O’Hare. American’s filing goes further – it asks to dismiss the entire lawsuit with prejudice, including its claim for money damages. Chicago and United don’t object, and each side would bear its own costs and legal fees. Once approved, that closes the door on American returning to collect damages over the same 2025 gate redistribution. American Is Choosing To Drop The Case Earlier today I explained that losing the appeal didn’t end American’s lawsuit. The appeals court upheld the denial of a preliminary injunction because it accepted that undoing the gate changes would cause greater disruption than leaving them in place. It didn’t finally decide whether Chicago breached the 2018 lease, or whether doing so damaged American. The airline is now choosing to stop pursuing that underlying case. The airline maintains that the 2025 process violated its agreement and gave United an unfair head start, but says the changed circumstances at O’Hare make investing and competing there a better focus. I still think American has the better contract argument. The city promised additional gate capacity and a protected period to grow into it before another redistribution. The trial judge accepted that the promise had been made, but suggested that even if Chicago was breaking that promise it might not be enforceable. But the evidence in the case was pretty clear that Chicago was redistributing gates earlier than they’d promised to, and that the timing was part of American’s bargained-for consideration in signing the lease. I was skeptical from the beginning that American would get an injunction, because its losses seemed potentially compensable with money. But I also suggested that American had recovered its gate position so the value in litigation seemed almost beside the point at this point. More Flights, More Destinations, And Gates Coming Back Before American sued, it planned forup to 480 daily departures and a network of about 150 destinations. Summer 2025 represented 22% more departures and 25% more seats than the prior year. American now has more than 500 daily departures and service to more than 185 destinations in 20 countries and territories. Chicago is its third-largest hub, with nearly 10,000 employees. And their spring 2026 schedule called for more than 500 peak daily departures, with 30% more departures than spring 2025. American counts more than 30 new destinations added or announced from Chicago since the start of 2025. Naples launched in May 2025 and Honolulu that October. Maui starts December 17, while Tokyo Narita starts March 19, 2027. This growth earned back gate space in this October’s redistribution. Separately, it paid $30 million for Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases, which I was first to report. A Bigger Admirals Club And Better Facilities The new L concourse Admirals Club will replace American’s smallest and weakest O’Hare lounge next year. The current space is basically a sad room with a bar and a small conference room. It’s convenient to the L gates, but it isn’t much of a reason to choose American. The replacement will exceed 10,000 square feet and double the current footprint, with floor-to-ceiling windows, airfield views, and the newer design American has introduced in places like Washington National, Denver, Newark, and Philadelphia. The existing club remains open during construction. American’s rendering shows what they’re building: Refurbished gates K1 and L2A have reopened with larger waiting areas, and baggage claim carousels 30 through 33 are operating. American has also invested in the product passengers get once they board: Its O’Hare operation now offers a premium cabin on every flight, after replacing single class regional jets with aircraft offering first class and Wi-Fi. Chicago received the new Boeing 787-9s with 51 business class suites first. United Still Has To Compete With American In Chicago United wanted American to back away from O’Hare. Scott Kirby talked up American’s losses and tried to get financial analysts to pressure the airline to retreat. United filed more flying to keep American from improving its gate position, even though it didn’t independently want all of that additional capacity. The Federal Aviation Administration concluded that the airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines had filed. Its summer flight caps used approved 2025 schedules as the baseline, rather than rewarding United for its much bigger proposed buildup. That protected American’s competitive position. The federal intervention and American’s recovered gate space have mattered more to its ability to stay and grow than the injunction appeal. American still has to make the flying work. But Kirby’s preferred answer—have American leave so United can dominate—would also cost American connecting traffic, local customers, and credit card spending. The airline tells me it’s seeing growth in local and business customers, AAdvantage enrollments, and credit card acquisitions. It’s also bringing in Margaret Mueller, former head of the Executives’ Club of Chicago, as vice president and managing partner for the market starting November 30. Her job includes local sales and business relationships. That’s where the larger schedule and lounge spending have to pay off. Chicago is one of the biggest credit card spending markets in the country. American needs a schedule customers can use and an experience they’ll choose if it wants them earning AAdvantage miles on their everyday spending. The new Admirals Club also gives them a more tangible reason to keep paying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive card. Refurbished gates K1 and L2A have reopened with larger waiting areas, and baggage claim carousels 30 through 33 are operating. American has also invested in the product passengers get once they board:

United wanted American to back away from O’Hare. Scott Kirby talked up American’s losses and tried to get financial analysts to pressure the airline to retreat. United filed more flying to keep American from improving its gate position, even though it didn’t independently want all of that additional capacity. The Federal Aviation Administration concluded that the airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines had filed. Its summer flight caps used approved 2025 schedules as the baseline, rather than rewarding United for its much bigger proposed buildup. That protected American’s competitive position. The federal intervention and American’s recovered gate space have mattered more to its ability to stay and grow than the injunction appeal. American still has to make the flying work. But Kirby’s preferred answer—have American leave so United can dominate—would also cost American connecting traffic, local customers, and credit card spending. The airline tells me it’s seeing growth in local and business customers, AAdvantage enrollments, and credit card acquisitions. It’s also bringing in Margaret Mueller, former head of the Executives’ Club of Chicago, as vice president and managing partner for the market starting November 30. Her job includes local sales and business relationships. That’s where the larger schedule and lounge spending have to pay off. Chicago is one of the biggest credit card spending markets in the country. American needs a schedule customers can use and an experience they’ll choose if it wants them earning AAdvantage miles on their everyday spending. The new Admirals Club also gives them a more tangible reason to keep paying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive card. Litigation is quite often a pressure point. In this matter, American may have lost the case (or is choosing not to pursue further), but gained significant benefits from having brought the litigation and keeping the pressure on. It doesn’t sound like from this article that any formal settlement was reached over this matter, but it did demonstrate to the powers that be in Chicago that AA is serious about competing at ORD and is not going anywhere.

American won by not giving up and refocusing its efforts on being relevant in Chicago.

Their new management has a “we have to fight to win” mindset that they will need in Chicago more than any other market.

The real question is where Chicago comes in priority compared to other opportunities; AA has lost share in NYC, BOS and LAX among large markets that are competitive w/ DL and UA. I don’t think AA has the bandwidth or the earnings to take on all of those markets and win given that UA and esp. DL have much higher earnings.

UA”s earnings will continue to be diluted because of having to fight against AA where average fares are much lower than competing hubs such as DTW and MSP as well as ATL and DFW.

in an industry where air travel is increasingly concentrating around the big 4, AA cannot afford to give up any more share and has to claw back what it can.

Man, I really want American to come back. They seem to have a change in attitude and perspective and intelligence. I hope it’s for real. I hope it sticks.

The terms of this ORD gate allocation agreement have been grossly misunderstood and misrepresented. The tell-tale sign is “without prejudice.” That horse has been dead so you can stop beating it.

UA has gone from a 6% market share lead in 2019 at ORD to 18% in 2026. UA’s advantages will grow with their Starlink & United Next completion in 2027, the 2028 completion of the ORD D concourse & the E concourse phase 1 in 2030.

A Deutsche Bank analysis in February estimated UA generates about $10 billion of annual revenue tied to Chicago, compared with just over $5 billion for AA, and put UA’s 2025 operating margin in the market at about 5% vs an estimated negative 9%-10% for American.

@Gary: Some of us pointed out the flaw in your legal analysis was leaving out the fact that it’s Chicago.

It had nothing to do with Chicago and everything to do with armchair legal analysis.

@rebel – no court has disagreed with my legal analysis in this case

American couldn’t get an injunction. Their contract analysis is more persuasive, but the damages are compensable. That’s what I wrote from the start, and every court decision has been consistent with this.

Sorry Gary, but as you said AAL’s “filing goes further – it asks to dismiss the entire lawsuit with prejudice, including its claim for money damages.” This means AAL is permanently giving up any their claims in this case. Why would AAL just give up their substantial claim to compensatory monetary ($) damages unless they know that the trigger for the ORD gate reallocation was in December 2023 when UAL said it was and not in March of 2025 when the AA ORD L concourse ‘Stinger’ gates became operational? This is overwhelming prima facie evidence that AAL has zero belief in the strength of their underlying case.

Sorry, your tortured dog of a legal argument don’t hunt.

#6071. Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights

The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused issues for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:

The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:

Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”

Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

#6070. Delta Holding December 2 Seattle Event To Announce New Singapore Flight—And Pick A Fight With Its Former Partner

Delta Air Lines is throwing an Asian night market in Seattle on December 2, where they’ll finally reveal non-stop Singapore service. That would put Delta into a roughly 17 hour nonstop fight with Singapore Airlines, giving its customers a way to reach one of Asia’s most important business centers without changing planes in Seoul. Enilria reported the December 2 Seattle announcement several days ago and highlighted the invitation’s Asian theme. Aviation watchdog JonNYC has now corroborated that direction, reporting that the event has an “Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme,” then adding: “Singapore as in.” Heard the Delta Seattle event has an Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 23, 2026 The invitation is for Delta Night Market at MOPOP, Seattle’s Museum of Pop Culture, on Wednesday, December 2 from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. It promises food, drinks, shopping and cultural experiences built around Asian destinations, along with city-inspired charms guests can collect. The line that caught Enilria’s attention: Seven destinations. One unforgettable night. Delta’s current and announced East and Southeast Asian destinations are Tokyo, Seoul, Shanghai, Taipei, Hong Kong and Manila. That’s seven airports when you count both Tokyo Haneda and Narita, but six cities. If they’re counting cities, Singapore makes seven. So I don’t take this to mean seven new routes, though of course there may be additional routes announced. . And there’s a more concrete clue than the party theme. In a July 29 presentation to a Pacific air traffic coordination group, Delta wrote: New markets announced for 2027 are Manila and Singapore. This Has Been Coming For More Than A Year I reported Delta’s plans to return to Singapore and Manila in October 2025. The following month, I wrote about their internal view that Europe was already pretty full, and that future long haul growth would lean heavily toward Asia, from both Los Angeles and Seattle. JonNYC has been all over this story. In August, Delta revealed at an event for its largest corporate customers that Singapore would follow closely behind Manila. Los Angeles–Manila is scheduled to begin March 28, 2027, initially three times weekly before going daily June 7. Delta last served Singapore in September 2019, as a flight from Tokyo Narita. They dismantled the connecting hub inherited from Northwest, moved their U.S.–Tokyo flying to Haneda and relied more heavily on Korean Air’s Seoul hub to get passengers elsewhere in Asia. Singapore Is A Market Delta Needs To Sell Singapore combines regional headquarters, finance, technology and a wealthy local market. For the multinational business traffic Delta wants, it has become more important than Hong Kong. There are now several times as many regional corporate headquarters in Singapore than Hong Kong. Hong Kong remains a major destination for the Greater Bay Area of China, while Singapore is where companies increasingly put the people managing businesses across the region. Plus, even for the China market Singapore increasingly matters. It’s the first stop for Nvidia chips before moving to Malaysia. Men just want to be seen 😂 https://t.co/a32B5SSQlV — Autism Capital 🧩 (@AutismCapital) November 10, 2026 Delta has been pushing Singapore traffic through Seoul on Korean Air. But a Seattle business traveler isn’t going to want that over a nonstop on Singapore Airlines, or for that matter the entire West Coast market is better served with a Singapore Airlines connection through Seattle, San Francisco or Los Angeles. Those choices can affect domestic flying and credit card spending as well. Meanwhile, Seattle is a shorter trip to Singapore than Los Angeles, which helps with fuel burn and payload on an already very long route. And Alaska is becoming a long haul competitor. It has announced Osaka and Tahiti for 2027, taking its announced Seattle intercontinental network to nine destinations, with a goal of at least 15 by 2030. Delta’s recent additions of Rome and Tokyo Narita have gone directly after Alaska. Singapore would give Delta a destination Alaska doesn’t fly itself. Delta has already invested in a Delta One Lounge and more gate access in Seattle. Adding a long business route gives them another way to sell that investment. The Seattle lounge photo below is courtesy of Delta. Delta’s Pacific Growth Hasn’t Produced Great Passenger Results I wrote last month that Delta’s Pacific passenger performance was trailing United and even American. Airline   Pacific passenger revenue per available seat mile, Q3 2026 vs. Q3 2025 Delta Air Lines   +5% United Airlines   +10.9% American Airlines   +11.3% Delta added 8% more Pacific capacity, while the share of seats filled fell two percentage points. Over two years, they added about 16% more flying while passenger revenue per seat mile barely moved. However, Delta reported $959 million in total Pacific operating revenue for the quarter against $756 million in passenger revenue. That’s another $203 million. Including it, total revenue per seat mile grew roughly 10%, rather than 5%. Delta doesn’t break out how much of that regional difference comes from cargo versus international joint venture settlements. Singapore has greater potential than adding a second Tokyo airport to go after Alaska. And it’s a stronger business market than Manila. There’s also an historical irony in taking on Singapore Airlines. The two airlines used to be partners. Singapore bought a 5% stake in Delta in 1989 and sold it a decade later, but their frequent flyer relationship lasted until May 2010. Back then, the best use of SkyMiles was redeeming for Singapore Airlines first class. There’s only so much Pacific growth Delta can do with this widebody delivery timeline:

2027: 8 A350-1000s 2028: 10 A350-1000s 2029: A350-900s (some of 15 start), A330-900neo (some of 16 start) 2030: (probably receive remainder of A350-900 and A330-900neo orders) 2031: 787-10 (first of 30 orders – so, maybe 10?) 3032: Maybe next 10 787-10s? 3033: Maybe final 10 787-10s?

Only American is worse off, as they are considering a new order – and will presumably have to wait even longer to see any new jets if they place one. They are only getting their remaining 19 787s in 2027 and 2028.

United, of course, is receiving the most widebodies the soonest- roughly 140 within the next 4-5 years, compared to Delta’s +/- 55 and American’s 19 over the same period.

That’s the problem with some of the “Here’s what Delta can do against the competition!” predictions. Those predictions are being based on what Delta will do IN THE FUTURE vs. what the competition is doing NOW. It’s easy to see the flaw in that type of analysis.

Instead, if those 140 widebodies for United replace existing planes, you’ve soon have new 787s vs old 767-300s. Easy to guess which will appeal to customers more. If they don’t replace existing planes, you’ll have growth nobody can match – growth that might giving multiple, convenient options to popular destinations, or a route network to locations nobody else can offer. Or most likely both.

United’s bet to place a big order coming out of the pandemic sure looks like it will pay off well for them.

Yes, but only if you choose not to travel. U.S. Department of Transportation rules require airlines to issue prompt refunds to passengers whose flight is canceled or significantly delayed. But passengers aren't eligible for a refund if they take a later flight.

Yes. DOT refund rules govern all flight disruptions, even flights canceled or delayed because of bad weather.

If the airline owes you a refund, federal rules require the carrier to refund your money within seven days if you paid by credit card, or 20 days if you paid by a different means.

It's been a chaotic couple of weeks for air travel in America, between tech outages and bad weather. Now, the holiday rush is here.

And with millions of travelers heading to airports, it's an important time to brush up on one of the most important rights that passengers have: getting a refund.

In the U.S., passengers don't have a ton of protection when it comes to delays and cancellations.

However, the federal government does have clear rules about when an airline must issue a refund.

Let's quickly walk through when you're owed a refund — and when you're not — so you can know what to ask for the next time you encounter flight trouble.

Read more: Is air travel ready for the holidays? The meltdown is over, but worries persist

For domestic flights, as well as international flights departing or arriving in the U.S., you’re covered by the rules of the U.S. Department of Transportation.

Under the DOT flight refund policy, you are entitled to a refund, no questions asked, if your flight is canceled and you ultimately choose not to travel. It doesn’t matter whether the cancellation was the airline’s fault or due to something beyond its control, like bad weather.

The policy applies to any unflown portion of your ticket.

The DOT refund rules also apply when a flight is significantly delayed or when the airline makes a significant schedule change.

Again, though, this is only if you choose not to travel.

According to federal law, a significant delay occurs when a domestic flight arrives at its destination at least three hours late, or an international flight arrives six hours late.

That also applies when the airline decides to change a flight's schedule.

Here's the big catch: You're only owed a refund if you choose not to travel, and you don't accept rebooking.

Your right to a refund is helpful if you run into a flight cancellation and delay and choose to:

The federal refund rules are less helpful if you need to fly to your destination and don't have a better backup option.

If your airline cancels your 8 a.m. flight and rebooks you on a later flight — even if it's a lot later —  your carrier would not technically owe you a refund if you agree to take that later flight.

In recent years, you may have heard about the federal government passing stricter rules when it comes to flight refunds.

That did happen, but the rules still aren't ironclad.

The actual criteria for when passengers are owed a refund didn't meaningfully change, though.

By law, airline refunds are expected "promptly" — within seven days for passengers who paid by credit card and within 20 days for those who paid by another means.

Airlines are allowed to offer passengers a voucher (or miles) instead of a refund.

However, refund-eligible passengers don’t have to accept a voucher. They can insist on simply getting their money back instead.

Know the fine print: Under the DOT's policy, if an airline wants to offer you miles when you're technically due a refund, they have to clearly disclose that.

Think carefully before accepting airline miles instead of a cash refund. You'll want to make sure you're truly getting better value. Consult TPG’s points and miles valuations to check the value of what the airline is offering in loyalty currency.

Remember: Airlines tend to devalue miles over time, so if you do accept miles, we'd suggest using them as soon as possible.

Compensation for things like meals, an unexpected hotel stay or an Uber ride in the event of a flight delay or cancellation falls under a different category than refunds.

Many airlines make guarantees about what they’ll provide in the event of a cancellation or significant delay. Those promises are laid out on the DOT’s airline customer service dashboard.

These promises are more discretionary forms of compensation. In other words, the airlines don't technically have to offer those meal vouchers or hotel bookings. Think of this as more of a goodwill gesture that the airlines have promised their customers they'll provide ... depending on the circumstances.

Also, airlines generally offer compensation only for hotel, meal and ground transportation when it's a "controllable" disruption — in other words, when it's the airline's fault.

I wouldn't count on that hotel voucher if your flight is canceled due to a winter storm or air traffic control delays.

This is where a credit card that offers travel insurance protections can be crucial (and, for me, really eliminates the financial stress of flight troubles).

Check out TPG’s guide to passenger rights for a better sense of what you might be owed.

Just prior to leaving office, the Biden administration proposed rules requiring airlines to pay passengers additional cash compensation when the carrier caused a cancellation or major delay.

However, the Trump administration opted not to move forward with that measure.

It can be challenging to keep track of airline policies, but the federal rules that govern refunds are relatively straightforward.

You are owed a refund for any unused portion of your ticket if your flight is canceled, significantly delayed or has a significant schedule change (no matter the reason) and you ultimately choose not to travel with that airline. That refund should come automatically and within seven days if you paid by credit card, or 20 days if you paid using a different method.

Passengers who feel that an airline hasn't followed protocol or has unfairly denied a refund request can file a complaint with the DOT.

#6067. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#6066. Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”

Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG

Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?

#6065. Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:

The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:

Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM

The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was launched in the first place, and is sticking around.

While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

#6064. Joe Biden Flew Cape Air For Thanksgiving—His Airport Cart Ride Turned Into A Political Fight

Joe Biden carried his bag through Philadelphia airport, got onto a police cart, and wound up at the center of another argument about the 2024 election. Biden and his wife Jill were headed to Nantucket for Thanksgiving. The final leg of the trip was on Cape Air. The former president turned 84 on Friday. He’s dealing with cancer. And he’s still traveling commercially with his wife, albeit with a security detail and a little more help getting through the terminal than most passengers receive. Shakiah Davis posted this video with the caption, “Ran into Joe and his wife today at the PHL…..” Biden walks slowly, carrying a tan leather duffel, then takes a seat on a Philadelphia Police electric cart. Jill is seated on another cart. Here’s the version without the political argument pasted over the footage: View Shakiah Davis’s video of Joe and Jill Biden at Philadelphia airport The Carry On store visible behind Biden is at the top of Philadelphia’s B concourse, next to Passyunk Steaks. This is familiar territory for American Airlines passengers. The Bidens arrived on Nantucket Sunday evening, November 22, on Cape Air from Boston. That was their arrival airline last Thanksgiving, too. Their family tradition of spending the holiday on the island dates to 1975, and they’re staying again at David Rubenstein’s waterfront property. View Nantucket Current’s video of the Bidens’ Thanksgiving arrival Earlier this month he explained why he was cutting back appearances for his new book: Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down. The version of the airport video reposted by Western Journal uses it to revisit claims that Biden could have handled another four years in office. The comments on the cleaner version include “Yeah, he could’ve served another 4 years” and Nick Shirley’s “Put him back in office he’s ready for another 4.” But “The guy is fighting cancer………” had more than 23,000 likes when I checked, substantially more than either of those comments. Even under the political repost, one response was, “Not a fan but will pray for him and his family.” I’ve long viewed Biden as an honorable man and a poor president. He let his administration operate like a feudal system, with interest groups controlling their policy areas. That made for bad policy and bad politics, pulling him away from the median voters who elected him. He also wasn’t up to another term. Pretending otherwise delayed a real process to choose his successor, and handing the nomination to Kamala Harris left his party poorly positioned for the election. She was a terrible candidate. But the debate made the problem clear, and he dropped out. A video of him taking an airport cart more than two years doesn’t tell us anything new. Now he’s an airline passenger going to see his family. In June 2025 he was flying United Airlines first class out of Houston. That December he was boarding American Airlines in Miami for St. Croix, standing in the boarding line with an escort. We could enjoy Jimmy Carter walking through a Delta Air Lines cabin and greeting passengers without agreeing about his presidency. Jimmy Carter greeting passengers aboard Delta Air Lines, June 8, 2017 George W. Bush gets more room to be a retired president, too (sometimes more from Democrats than from Trump Republicans, given the split between Trump and the Bush family). Enjoying an encounter with a former president doesn’t require revising your assessment of his time in office. There are still airline issues worth arguing about. In June 2025, I criticized American Airlines bumping a passenger from first class to accommodate Biden on flight 2717 from Minneapolis to Philadelphia. He’d been attending the funeral of murdered Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman. A former president’s scheduling preferences shouldn’t outrank someone else’s confirmed seat. If the airline needs room for his party, it can ask for volunteers and pay them enough to take a different seat or flight. It seems President Trump, who already owned aircraft before entering office, may have an ex-Qatari royal 747 at his disposal. Hopefully better judgment will prevail there. BushHand luggageHoustonJimmy CarterKamala HarrisMiamiMinneapolisMinnesotaNantucketPhiladelphiaPhiladelphia International AirportQatarSaint CroixUnited Airlines+19 more More From View from the Wing

The former president turned 84 on Friday. He’s dealing with cancer. And he’s still traveling commercially with his wife, albeit with a security detail and a little more help getting through the terminal than most passengers receive.

Shakiah Davis posted this video with the caption, “Ran into Joe and his wife today at the PHL…..” Biden walks slowly, carrying a tan leather duffel, then takes a seat on a Philadelphia Police electric cart. Jill is seated on another cart. Here’s the version without the political argument pasted over the footage:

View Shakiah Davis’s video of Joe and Jill Biden at Philadelphia airport

The Carry On store visible behind Biden is at the top of Philadelphia’s B concourse, next to Passyunk Steaks. This is familiar territory for American Airlines passengers. The Bidens arrived on Nantucket Sunday evening, November 22, on Cape Air from Boston. That was their arrival airline last Thanksgiving, too. Their family tradition of spending the holiday on the island dates to 1975, and they’re staying again at David Rubenstein’s waterfront property.

View Nantucket Current’s video of the Bidens’ Thanksgiving arrival

Earlier this month he explained why he was cutting back appearances for his new book:

Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.

The version of the airport video reposted by Western Journal uses it to revisit claims that Biden could have handled another four years in office. The comments on the cleaner version include “Yeah, he could’ve served another 4 years” and Nick Shirley’s “Put him back in office he’s ready for another 4.”

But “The guy is fighting cancer………” had more than 23,000 likes when I checked, substantially more than either of those comments. Even under the political repost, one response was, “Not a fan but will pray for him and his family.”

I’ve long viewed Biden as an honorable man and a poor president. He let his administration operate like a feudal system, with interest groups controlling their policy areas. That made for bad policy and bad politics, pulling him away from the median voters who elected him.

He also wasn’t up to another term. Pretending otherwise delayed a real process to choose his successor, and handing the nomination to Kamala Harris left his party poorly positioned for the election. She was a terrible candidate. But the debate made the problem clear, and he dropped out. A video of him taking an airport cart more than two years doesn’t tell us anything new. Now he’s an airline passenger going to see his family.

In June 2025 he was flying United Airlines first class out of Houston. That December he was boarding American Airlines in Miami for St. Croix, standing in the boarding line with an escort.

We could enjoy Jimmy Carter walking through a Delta Air Lines cabin and greeting passengers without agreeing about his presidency.

Jimmy Carter greeting passengers aboard Delta Air Lines, June 8, 2017

George W. Bush gets more room to be a retired president, too (sometimes more from Democrats than from Trump Republicans, given the split between Trump and the Bush family). Enjoying an encounter with a former president doesn’t require revising your assessment of his time in office.

There are still airline issues worth arguing about. In June 2025, I criticized American Airlines bumping a passenger from first class to accommodate Biden on flight 2717 from Minneapolis to Philadelphia. He’d been attending the funeral of murdered Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman.

A former president’s scheduling preferences shouldn’t outrank someone else’s confirmed seat. If the airline needs room for his party, it can ask for volunteers and pay them enough to take a different seat or flight. It seems President Trump, who already owned aircraft before entering office, may have an ex-Qatari royal 747 at his disposal. Hopefully better judgment will prevail there.

#6063. Thrifty Traveler Is 30% Off For Black Friday—A Year Of Flight And Business Class Award Alerts For $90.99

They tell me this is their biggest sale of the year, and the biggest they expect to offer for the foreseeable future. It matches the 30% discount I covered in August.

Readers who took advantage of the offer before their March price increase did better: $79 for the first year and $99 for renewals. That offer’s gone. The regular annual prices are now $129.99 and $189.99, and their price lock guarantee applies to those full prices, not the discounted first year.

I’ve said this is one of the better services for finding rare premium cabin awards. They search departures from more than 200 airports in the U.S. and Canada, and you choose which airports you want alerts for. You can stick to your home airport or include other cities you’re willing to position to.

Deals arrive by email, there’s an online hub where you can browse them, and you can opt into text alerts for mistake fares and their rarest “unicorn” deals. They say they’ve recently sent more than 80 flight alerts in a month, including more than 30 business class award alerts, such as:

Most alerts won’t fit any one person’s plans. I like this most for someone with transferable points who can let award availability help decide where to go. Finding one useful business class award can easily justify the subscription. If you need a particular flight on a particular date, though, a stream of deals to other places isn’t going to solve that.

They’ve also added FareTracker. Premium members can track up to 10 cash flights and get an email when the price drops by at least $20, with instructions to rebook and claim the difference as an airline credit. You still need a fare whose rules allow that, and you have to do the rebooking. But it’s a useful reason to keep watching a ticket after you’ve bought it.

The Premium+ bundle adds hotel deals, including difficult award availability and discounted paid stays. Recent alerts have included Park Hyatt Kyoto and the renovated Waldorf Astoria New York. The extra $42 makes sense if you’d build a trip around finding award nights at a property like that.
