#6062. Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card

Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:

Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:

If you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

The Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being said, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

The card also has no extra cost to add authorized users, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:

Personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

As Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

Southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

Preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

The Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

Extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

Keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

On your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

In other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

If you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

Many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

That said, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

First, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:

The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:

I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

If you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

Should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

When providing credit card advice, my answer to whether or not it makes sense to get a certain card is usually “it depends.” and this is the case as well with the Southwest Priority Card, especially given the latest changes to the Southwest Rapid Rewards program.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

If you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later. Southwest credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward Companion Pass qualification in 2027, and this card’s 90,000-point welcome offer can get you a good chunk of the way there.

Have you ever butted heads with a partner because you wanted to plan a jam-packed vacation itinerary and they preferred to lounge on the beach? Have you ever argued with family or friends about whether to book a local Airbnb or an all-inclusive resort? When flying solo, you don't need to worry about these dilemmas — and that's far from the only benefit of solo travel.

However, planning a trip on your own can feel daunting, especially if it's your first time. That's why I've rounded up some of TPG's favorite destinations for first-time solo travelers. No matter what kind of traveler you are and what you're looking for on your maiden voyage, this list is sure to inspire you.

Related: The 12 best places to travel solo

While Mexico often conjures images of all-inclusive hotels and long beach days, the cultural and culinary hub of Oaxaca goes deeper. TPG managing editor Lyndsey Matthews just got back from a solo trip here and raves about the travel-worthy food scene and captivating art and history.

“The historic center of Oaxaca is easily walkable and full of coffee shops, art galleries and ceramic stores to pop in and out of at your own pace and convenience,” she says. “It was also super easy to make friends on the few tours I booked — I did a nighttime street food tour with Culinary Backstreets and a long day trip to Hierve del Agua that I booked on Viator, and I ended up running into the people I met at bakeries and markets the rest of the week.”

Related: 5 detour destinations in Mexico beyond the tourist hot spots

Whatever type of solo trip you’re dreaming of, France is worth considering.

TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson recommends Paris. It may be known as the City of Love, but that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy it on your own — especially if you’re a foodie or art lover. Snack on fresh-baked croissants in between museum visits (the Musee du quai Branly, which features non-Western art from around the world, is a must-see).

If you’d prefer a slower pace, Lauren Wassum raves about Provence: “There are plenty of villages to explore where you can get in touch with yourself through slow and intentional living.” But this isn’t to say there is nothing to do. “You can walk Van Gogh’s footsteps in Arles and Saint-Rémy, take a provencal cooking class or even tour the lavender fields when in they are in bloom in the Luberon Valley.”

To really push yourself out of your comfort zone, try Japan for your first solo trip. Japan’s culture and traditions are so different from the U.S., it will catapult you out of your day-to-day life a little faster than most destinations.

TPG senior writer Tanner Saunders loves the Land of the Rising Sun as a solo destination. “Tokyo is massive, sure, but it's relatively easy to figure out how to get around, the people are mostly so kind, it's super safe and dining alone is so common.” And don’t worry if you can’t read Japanese; English is common in most tourist areas.

Japan may seem small, but its islands are incredibly diverse. There’s something for every type of traveler — from the snow-dusted ski capital of Hokkaido to the southernmost island of Okinawa, sometimes known as “the Hawaii of Japan.”

Related: When is the best time to visit Japan?

Senior editor Christine Gallipeau recommends New Zealand for first-time solo travelers, citing the country’s safety record and the Kiwis’ trademark friendliness.

“I was there during the Rugby World Cup and had a last-minute issue with lodging,” she says. “One of the local airports let me and my friends just crash in the rental car office for the night, and later in Wellington, a stranger opened their home to us since hostels and hotels were sold out.”

It takes a while to get here, but you’ll be rewarded with peace, quiet and the sense of being truly alone.

Most visitors agree road tripping is the best way to see New Zealand, so you’ll need to rent a car (and be prepared to drive on the left side). You can see the highlights in just a few days, or spend weeks exploring and not run out of things to do.

Related: Explore some of New Zealand's most beautiful regions at these Rosewood lodges

If you’d like to stay a little closer to home for your first solo trip, Costa Rica is relatively easy to reach from the U.S. while still feeling a world away.

It’s among Latin America’s most popular solo travel destinations thanks, in part, to its friendly locals. “Everyone is sooo welcoming,” says TPG social media manager Maren Gimnes, “plus it’s safe and easy to get around.”

With beaches on one side and wildlife-rich rainforests on the other, not to mention volcanoes and hot springs, solo travelers can get their fill of both relaxation and adventure.

Try basing yourself in Tamarindo if you’re after sun, surf and sand. If wildlife is your main goal, head to Monteverde Cloud Forest or Manuel Antonio National Park. Thrill seekers will want to focus on La Fortuna, the country’s adventure capital.

Related: How to visit Costa Rica on points and miles

Many European cities are great candidates for first-time solo trips, but Ireland’s lively capital city stands out for its welcoming pub culture and manageable size. TPG social media manager Annie Black loves it because Dublin is “very easy to navigate and has lots of fun free things to do.”

If you’re hoping to socialize with locals and fellow travelers, Dublin’s welcoming pub culture is a must. Head to the bustling Temple Bar neighborhood (or any pub, really) for a pint of Guinness or Bulmer’s and some foot-stomping trad music.

Plus, plentiful day trips and group tours make it easy for solo travelers to explore nearby attractions like the gorgeous Wicklow Mountains and the jaw-dropping Giant’s Causeway without the hassle of renting a car.

Related: What it's like flying Aer Lingus business class across the Atlantic

If you’re ready to venture a little farther afield, TPG principal Eric Rosen highlights Cape Town as a great spot for first-time visitors, saying it’s “very navigable and safe for solo travelers.”

Cape Town has all the benefits of a city trip plus easy access to outdoor pursuits like hiking, mountain bike trails, beaches and even penguins. Rideshares are readily available and affordable for getting around town, or you can easily explore outside the city by renting a car, hiring a driver or joining an organized group tour.

Sea Point and De Waterkant/Green Point neighborhoods are great choices for solo travelers wanting a safe, walkable base close to the beach. If you’d rather be within easy reach of the restaurant and bar scene on Kloof Street, try Tamboerskloof.

Related: Africa's first Edition hotel is opening in Cape Town next year

Vietnam is a Southeast Asian sliver of adventure, culture and more. Plus, it’s quite affordable — even if you’re not splitting the cost of your hotel with a travel companion. Most meals will run you between $5 and $10.

There’s truly something for everyone: The UNESCO World Heritage Site of Ha Long Bay; the delightfully chaotic capital of Hanoi; and the hip beach town of Da Nang, where expats from all over the world relax.

You won’t want to leave without sampling some of the local cuisine. There’s pho and banh mi, of course, but don’t miss other local dishes like bun cha (pork with dipping broth) and cha ca (turmeric-marinated fish). Wash it all down with a beer at Hanoi’s Train Street, where you can eat while watching an active railway run back and forth inches from your trackside café.

Related: A new Hilton just opened one of Vietnam's best cities

There’s a reason (several, in fact) that Iceland is a perennial favorite for solo travelers. English is nearly ubiquitous, and the country’s manageable size and well-developed infrastructure make it easy to get around. It’s also one of the safest countries on the planet — so safe, it’s said Iceland has more horses than police officers.

Nature lovers can bask in a huge variety of landscapes, from hiking across glaciers to soaking in geothermal hot springs to snorkeling between tectonic plates. Meanwhile, travelers seeking nightlife and connection can revel in downtown Reykjavik, which also has a booming LGBTQIA+ scene.

“You really can’t go wrong with any Nordic country,” TPG managing editor Lyndsey Matthews says. “English is widely spoken, plus they’re all very safe countries, so I’ve always been comfortable whether it’s a super remote destination or a big city.”

Related: Delta Air Lines adds Iceland nonstops from Boston hub

Whether you’re looking for epic underwater adventures or a few days of beach bumming, look no further than the Central American oasis of Belize.

Despite its small size, Belize has a big reputation for some of the world’s best snorkeling and scuba diving. Check some adventures off your bucket list by diving the Great Blue Hole or swimming with nurse sharks in Shark Ray Alley.

If you’d rather spend your vacation on land — perhaps in a hammock with a good book and a cold drink — head out on a ferry to one of the many islands, or cays, like car-free Caye Caulker. The island's motto is “Go Slow,” and that’s all you need to know.

Related: Belize's best all-inclusive resorts

When traveling solo, you can go, do, see and eat exactly what you choose — whether that's a culture-filled city trip, an epic outdoor adventure, a relaxing beach break or a little of everything. This list has all the above so you can choose your dream solo destination.

Need more inspo for your first solo trip? Don't miss our roundups of the best places to travel solo in the US, the top destinations for a solo weekend getaway and the best cruise lines for solo travelers.

#6060. Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

Love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

That said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

After a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself…

Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

Getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

The screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

However, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

Ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

Oh, what a wonderfully outdated article! By all means, you do you, but this is such an oversimplification that it's almost funny. Nowadays, Ryanair is an absolutely mainstream airline. I personally know C-level execs who opt to fly Ryanair if it saves them a transfer in Frankfurt or London. There are heads of state in Europe that fly Ryanair for personal travel! You know why? Anyway, of course you do not need to fly Ryanair, but for us who are not so entitled it works very well ;)

None of the reasons you give make sense (other than engagement-bait) for why you'd title this piece and argue Why I'll Never Fly Ryanair. But Porto to Dublin at 10:00am should be fine, right? I've done BFS-EDI and STN-CPH and both were fine. Not my favorite experience, but totally fine

The argument doesn't make sense. It might be more expensive, it might be further out. But what about when it's not? You can tell these things before you book. Most of their airports are in the city these days. Likewise, if I want to get from Dublin to Poland, for example, there is no competition. Why would I take an indirect flight? I checked Wroclaw yesterday and it was four (!!!) flights to get there on Lufthansa.

It's nice to see your point of view on this Daniel! I'm a (younger) American, and when in the US, I typically avoid Frontier (and Spirit before) for similar reasons. The price difference was small (if I needed a cabin bag), and I preferred the small upcharge for a much better experience with legacy airlines. When I was studying abroad in London & Madrid (relatively recently - like I said, I am pretty young), I stuck to award flights on the legacy airlines a lot of the time, because the LLC flight costs were basically the same for the flights I needed (which were quick weekend getaways, leaving Friday after class and back Sun night/Mon morning). That allowed me to save a lot of time and money on transportation to/from secondary airports. That said, if I was looking to get between two secondary cities, often the LLC's nonstop flights were extremely convenient. But I was more of a tourist, so I was always down for an adventure no matter what.

#6059. New FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”

The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:

The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major issues, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy

While the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉

As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

What do you make of the FAA’s new restrictions on takeoff?

#6057. BermudAir Adding Flights All Over The Place: I Don’t Know What’s Going On

BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The company has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

For a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

Several months back, BermudAir announced new winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:

On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets:

Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed…

I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:

I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these new markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:

What’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know…

It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced new routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”

What do you make of BermudAir’s latest expansion?

Doesn’t BermudAir, or a subsidiary, have some special rights to fly to various Caribbean islands since Bermuda is tied to the UK? I’m sure not all the dots and lines will work out, but I hope enough of them do!

Airports fill up with travelers, Thanksgiving meals get prepped.

But for flyers hoping to do some cooking before their flight, there are important rules to know.

The Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy is still in place.

And, yes: It applies to some of the top items you may be thinking of bringing along on your trip, from the cranberry sauce to the jar of gravy.

“It’s weird, but sometimes we will see turkeys at security checkpoints,” former TSA spokesperson Mark Howell once told me.

That means extra work for TSA officers, who already have to contend with one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

Last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports.

If you’re among the travelers hoping to do a little meal prep at home before flying, there are some things you need to know — whether you’ll be waiting in the standard line (arrive early, if so) or heading to the TSA PreCheck line.

Read more: Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist

As always, the TSA’s 3-1-1 rule governs what can and can’t come through security.

If what you're packing doesn't meet that criteria, it needs to go in a checked bag if you want to fly with it.

Most travelers know they can’t bring a huge bottle of sunscreen in their carry-on luggage. However, things get a bit more confusing when we start talking Thanksgiving entrees and side dishes.

Related: When will the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids policy end?

Let’s start with the obvious here: You have to follow the 3-1-1 rule whether you’re bringing on a mini bottle of toothpaste or your family’s famous Thanksgiving side dish.

That means you’re good to bring a turkey, ham, chicken or something similar. Just keep in mind that the U.S. Department of Agriculture advises that you give special attention to packing and storing perishables — no one wants to eat a dish that spoiled during your flight.

You can keep your food cool with ice packs, but they must stay frozen through the checkpoint.

If you're bringing a frozen turkey, that also must be frozen when you pass through security. Your best bet: Leave it in the freezer until the moment you leave for the airport.

Other safe bets: You're generally clear to bring stuffing, macaroni and cheese, casseroles, pies, pastries, and fresh fruits and vegetables through the checkpoint. Just be aware they may get a second look or a second trip through the X-ray machine.

With many other classic holiday dishes, you’ll want to consider the ingredients before you try to carry them on. In some cases, it’s a pretty obvious “no-go.”

TSA officers have historically said that if you can "pump it, pour it, spray it or spread it," it needs to be checked — if it's more than 3.4 ounces.

Luckily, if you’re unsure what food can come on the plane, there are a few ways to confirm before your trip.

If your item falls into the “no” category for a carry-on bag, you should still be able to pack it in your checked luggage. This is a good time to use those free checked bags and other airline credits available on that travel credit card in your wallet.

Every time the TSA catches a prohibited item while scanning a bag, it causes a delay at the checkpoint. During what’s expected to be one of the busiest weeks of the year, those delays can add up.

Whether you plan to pack a bottle of hair gel or your family’s traditional Thanksgiving casserole, consider whether the size and composition of your item make it eligible to pass through security.

On the bright side, travelers no longer have to take off their shoes when passing through security.

#6054. Why Airport Food Costs So Much—High Rents, Costly Operations And Price Rules Shops Get To Work Around

A $7 bottle of airport water is bad enough. Being told the airport protects you from excessive prices, while it approves the price and collects money from the shop, is actually worse. There’s a new, good investigation into airport food prices with the reporter comparing terminal prices with stores outside the airport, then confronting the people supposedly enforcing the rules that prices are supposed to match. Airports usually defended the prices. I detest the hypocrisy here, but the video largely dismisses the economics that explain those rules, the exceptions, and the weak enforcement. Those are the reasons we get both the pricing promises and the prices that don’t match. Airports make concessions expensive to operate, then collect money from businesses selling to passengers who have limited alternatives. The starting point is understanding that passengers aren’t the customer, they’re the product. The Airport Sells Access To You An airport sells merchants access to people who have already cleared security, can’t easily leave, and may have only 20 minutes before boarding. You can compare restaurants, and if you did the different brands are often run by the same company with products sourced from the same vendor. And airport concession agreements frequently include not just rent but the greater of a minimum guaranteed payment or a percentage of sales. The airport wants successful merchants. Their sales support its budget. And airlines can benefit, too. Dallas–Fort Worth’s 2025 budget showed $120.1 million of non-airline net revenue going toward terminal costs and another $23.9 million toward airfield costs, reducing what airlines otherwise had to pay. That money came from parking but also concessions like restaurants. I’ve written about airports treating passengers as the product for years. The clearest example is removing moving walkways so people stop bypassing the shops. Dallas–Fort Worth approved a roughly $1 million project to remove walkways in terminal D and add retail and restaurant seating. The airport’s concessions executive said the project was expected to generate about $2 million in revenue within two years. Similarly, United removed the eight moving walkways inside Chicago O’Hare’s C concourse. Getting you to your gate efficiently and getting you to wander into shops and spend money are in tension, and there’s a strong preference for the latter. Street Pricing Depends On Which Street You Choose Many airports promise that vendors will charge the same prices as comparable businesses outside the airport, or those prices plus an allowed premium. The airport industry’s 2025 concessions survey found street pricing plus a percentage at 80% of responding large hubs. Chicago’s sample concession agreement calls for value pricing tied to approved off-airport stores, without a general percentage premium. The Port Authority Of New York New Jersey’s manual uses three to six approved comparison locations. Branded restaurants and shops generally must be compared with locations of the same brand. In the video, the Port Authority defends a $6.89 bottle of water by saying Hudson is a specialty market rather than a bodega. That’s especially rich given that its own manual describes travel essentials shops as also being known as news and gift shops or convenience stores, and specifically requires comparisons for bottled drinks and snacks. At Denver, most of the high prices out of sync with off-airport were expressly approved by the airport. Airport Starbucks are often compared to other airports rather than non-airport locations. You Can’t Wish Away The Cost Of Operating Inside An Airport I’ve explained why airport restaurants are expensive to operate. Rent is only part of it. Hiring is harder. Employees have to get to the airport, often park remotely and take a shuttle, clear security, and have to pass background checks. That limits the pool of available workers, makes the job less attractive, and drives up wages needed to attract employees. Deliveries require more handling. Supplies have to be screened and brought through controlled routes and delivery windows. Some airports require centralized distribution. DFW just opened a 90,000 square foot receiving and distribution center. Screening, facilities and handling and third parties that manage those add costs. Space and construction are expensive. There’s limited storage, kitchens face airport constraints, and building or renovating behind security is harder than fitting out a storefront in a strip mall. The airport controls the operating schedule. Merchants may have to open early and serve late flights even when those hours aren’t profitable. High prices at peak cross-subsidize slow times where merchants must remain open. The video answers the cost argument largely by pointing to high passenger volume. But merchants bid for that valuable traffic, and some of the benefit gets captured by the airport through rent and concession payments. Nor is expensive rent entirely an outside force the airport suffers from. The airport is the landlord. It’s choosing how much revenue to extract, what operating conditions to impose, and which merchants get access to the passengers. Many airports impose even higher wage costs than the market would require on its own. That costs money, too. But since U.S. airports are predominanelty owned by government, there’s political pressure to claim that passengers are being protected from the high prices that result from the government airport’s own policies. Airports Even Approve Fees To Get Around Their Own Caps Sometimes there’s no need to fudge price comparisons to support higher pricing needed to cover an airport’s higher cost environment. The airport passes a rule to allow vendors to charge more on top of the allowed price. I’ve covered airports allowing surcharges alongside their street pricing rules. The Port Authority’s current regulation permits a separate employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%, on top of its street price plus 15% rule. (And that ‘wage and benefit fee’ doesn’t actually go to workers as such.) Earlier this month I covered a JFK self-checkout purchase of a $21.99 book carrying a 3% employee retention fee. I’ve also covered Minneapolis’s earlier 4.5% hospitality surcharge, with a sign explaining that it isn’t a tip: Then there’s the tip screen. In Austin, I couldn’t pay by card at self-checkout for a bottle of water without entering at least a penny as a tip. Zero wasn’t an option, and entering a tip manually rejected $0. A separate Austin self-checkout I flagged in January defaulted to 18% while adding a card processing surcharge. Portland Shows The Rules Can Work When The Whole Deal Works None of this means street pricing is useless, or that charging outside prices inside an airport is impossible. The video finds much closer compliance in Portland. And Portland hasn’t eliminated airport operating costs. Its 2024 convenience retail lease package combined street pricing with rent tiers of 18% to 22% of sales for locations past security, a separate 1% delivery fee, metered utilities and storage charges. And caps can restrain prices even when they’re imperfect. In February I covered a comparison of Starbucks prices across 24 airports: a grande coffee was $3 in Salt Lake City and $5.05 in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Los Angeles. Phoenix had dropped its street pricing requirement. That snapshot doesn’t isolate the effect of the rules (Los Angeles had a cap and was still expensive), but it certainly doesn’t suggest that removing limits makes airport coffee cheap. I’d much rather airports were honest about the bargain: we charge merchants for access to you, operating here costs more, and the revenue helps pay for the airport and can reduce airline costs. Most major U.S. airports are publicly owned. The politicians responsible don’t want to put their names on that message. So we get a promise of street pricing, an expansive definition of the street, and an employee benefits fee at the self-checkout. And then the politicians act shocked. Shocked! That’s especially rich given that its own manual describes travel essentials shops as also being known as news and gift shops or convenience stores, and specifically requires comparisons for bottled drinks and snacks. At Denver, most of the high prices out of sync with off-airport were expressly approved by the airport. Airport Starbucks are often compared to other airports rather than non-airport locations. You Can’t Wish Away The Cost Of Operating Inside An Airport I’ve explained why airport restaurants are expensive to operate. Rent is only part of it. Hiring is harder. Employees have to get to the airport, often park remotely and take a shuttle, clear security, and have to pass background checks. That limits the pool of available workers, makes the job less attractive, and drives up wages needed to attract employees. Deliveries require more handling. Supplies have to be screened and brought through controlled routes and delivery windows. Some airports require centralized distribution. DFW just opened a 90,000 square foot receiving and distribution center. Screening, facilities and handling and third parties that manage those add costs. Space and construction are expensive. There’s limited storage, kitchens face airport constraints, and building or renovating behind security is harder than fitting out a storefront in a strip mall. The airport controls the operating schedule. Merchants may have to open early and serve late flights even when those hours aren’t profitable. High prices at peak cross-subsidize slow times where merchants must remain open. The video answers the cost argument largely by pointing to high passenger volume. But merchants bid for that valuable traffic, and some of the benefit gets captured by the airport through rent and concession payments. Nor is expensive rent entirely an outside force the airport suffers from. The airport is the landlord. It’s choosing how much revenue to extract, what operating conditions to impose, and which merchants get access to the passengers. Many airports impose even higher wage costs than the market would require on its own. That costs money, too. But since U.S. airports are predominanelty owned by government, there’s political pressure to claim that passengers are being protected from the high prices that result from the government airport’s own policies. Airports Even Approve Fees To Get Around Their Own Caps Sometimes there’s no need to fudge price comparisons to support higher pricing needed to cover an airport’s higher cost environment. The airport passes a rule to allow vendors to charge more on top of the allowed price. I’ve covered airports allowing surcharges alongside their street pricing rules. The Port Authority’s current regulation permits a separate employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%, on top of its street price plus 15% rule. (And that ‘wage and benefit fee’ doesn’t actually go to workers as such.) Earlier this month I covered a JFK self-checkout purchase of a $21.99 book carrying a 3% employee retention fee. I’ve also covered Minneapolis’s earlier 4.5% hospitality surcharge, with a sign explaining that it isn’t a tip: Then there’s the tip screen. In Austin, I couldn’t pay by card at self-checkout for a bottle of water without entering at least a penny as a tip. Zero wasn’t an option, and entering a tip manually rejected $0. A separate Austin self-checkout I flagged in January defaulted to 18% while adding a card processing surcharge. Portland Shows The Rules Can Work When The Whole Deal Works None of this means street pricing is useless, or that charging outside prices inside an airport is impossible. The video finds much closer compliance in Portland. And Portland hasn’t eliminated airport operating costs. Its 2024 convenience retail lease package combined street pricing with rent tiers of 18% to 22% of sales for locations past security, a separate 1% delivery fee, metered utilities and storage charges. And caps can restrain prices even when they’re imperfect. In February I covered a comparison of Starbucks prices across 24 airports: a grande coffee was $3 in Salt Lake City and $5.05 in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Los Angeles. Phoenix had dropped its street pricing requirement. That snapshot doesn’t isolate the effect of the rules (Los Angeles had a cap and was still expensive), but it certainly doesn’t suggest that removing limits makes airport coffee cheap. I’d much rather airports were honest about the bargain: we charge merchants for access to you, operating here costs more, and the revenue helps pay for the airport and can reduce airline costs. Most major U.S. airports are publicly owned. The politicians responsible don’t want to put their names on that message. So we get a promise of street pricing, an expansive definition of the street, and an employee benefits fee at the self-checkout. And then the politicians act shocked. Shocked! An airport sells merchants access to people who have already cleared security, can’t easily leave, and may have only 20 minutes before boarding. You can compare restaurants, and if you did the different brands are often run by the same company with products sourced from the same vendor.

And airport concession agreements frequently include not just rent but the greater of a minimum guaranteed payment or a percentage of sales. The airport wants successful merchants. Their sales support its budget. And airlines can benefit, too.

Dallas–Fort Worth’s 2025 budget showed $120.1 million of non-airline net revenue going toward terminal costs and another $23.9 million toward airfield costs, reducing what airlines otherwise had to pay. That money came from parking but also concessions like restaurants.

I’ve written about airports treating passengers as the product for years. The clearest example is removing moving walkways so people stop bypassing the shops.

Dallas–Fort Worth approved a roughly $1 million project to remove walkways in terminal D and add retail and restaurant seating. The airport’s concessions executive said the project was expected to generate about $2 million in revenue within two years.

Similarly, United removed the eight moving walkways inside Chicago O’Hare’s C concourse. Getting you to your gate efficiently and getting you to wander into shops and spend money are in tension, and there’s a strong preference for the latter. Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. A good explanation but the MSP fee was removed in 2025.

The irony is that the vast majority of the elite buy nothing at airports. Almost all my food and drink needs are met by the lounges and Priority Pass restaurants, and only a fool goes shopping at an airport. So I don’t care what political nonsense goes on with the restaurants and shops. If I happen to be visiting a non-lounge airport, I just take basic steps to prepare for that. Like I have an empty water bottle with me.

You make a strong case for why vendor pricing at airports is elevated when compared to shops outside of an airport. It’s always best to avoid shopping at airports for these reasons. Of course, sometimes it can not be avoided, but even then one should attempt to minimize one’s purchases.

Let’s not forget the excessive profits flowing to the handful of airport concession operators that dominate both in the US and Europe.

I have been boycotting all purchases in the airport concourses as the prices are obscene. If there was a major increase in the number of persons also boycotting, then perhaps there will be some recognition of the price-gouging being endorsed by airport governments. The whole pricing system for air travel and ancillaries needs to be scrutinized and appropriate corrective measures taken. I tend to remember when railroads were the major passenger provider and there were price limits. Also the ancillary services in the train stations had prices very close to what you would pay if you left the station and walked across the street to make the same purchase.

Well, Gary, this piece truly explains why much time here is spent on talking about lounges. If you have access to a lounge, don’t kvetch about the shops and restaurants. And if you are not a member, make or buy some sammies before you get to the airport, and eat them at the boarding area. And bring an empty water bottle and fill it up after clearing security.

#6053. Trump accused of 'socialism, communism' after helping scandal-plagued Nvidia CEO reclaim top job

President Donald Trump predicted that Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, wouldn't be diminished by the scandal during an interview on Monday and said, "sex sells," when responding to a question about how the company would move forward.

FIRST ON FOX: Republicans blasted Democrats on the campaign trail for pushing a socialist and communist agenda, but President Donald Trump’s involvement in getting Jensen Huang’s old job back has some lawmakers claiming hypocrisy.

"This is as close to socialism, communism as I've ever seen," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital.

"I mean, it's essentially state planning of private economies, and it's a whole new level of hypocrisy," he continued. "But the Republican Party definition of socialism is any government program, or government power, as long as the president doesn't like it or use it."

Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang Tuesday morning after allegations that the tech executive had a handful of affairs, notably with an alleged Chinese spy, placing him back at the top of the chip juggernaut after two weeks out of the gig.

TRUMP ‘DIRECTLY AND INDIRECTLY’ INTERVENED TO GET NVIDIA’S CEO REINSTATED, POTUS SAYS

President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science during the "A New Golden Age" summit at the U.S. Institute of Peace, renamed The Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace by the Trump administration, in Washington, D.C., Oct. 8, 2026. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

The company’s chips power myriad technologies that the Trump administration has pinned as critical to national security, including data centers and artificial intelligence, which lawmakers fear would be disastrous to fall into the hands of the Chinese government.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who has been hawkish on China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, told Fox News Digital that the company’s board was "free to vote however they want, but the federal government owes the American people answers about what actually happened."

"This looks terrible on its face, and it drives home the need for Congress to be informed on the full impact of Jensen Huang’s actions on our national security and economy," Scott said. "Congress needs to be fully briefed on this as soon as possible, so we can take appropriate action if need be."

TRUMP OFFICIALS TOLD 'NOT TO STAB EACH OTHER' AMID DEMANDS NVIDIA DISPUTE BE PUT UNDER OATH IN CONGRESS

The company’s stock spiraled and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle raised national security concerns about China’s access to Nvidia’s chips. They have since pushed for stricter export control legislation and demanded that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify on the Hill.

Trump, in an appearance on CNBC shortly after the board’s announcement, said he didn’t believe Huang would have been reinstated without him as he lauded the stock market’s upward trend.

"The answer is no," Trump said. "I believe my intervention was very important."

The Trump administration has not been shy about turning the government into a pipeline to the corporate world. The Cato Institute found in a report released in October that the administration has equity stakes in about 40 companies — though Nvidia is notably not on the list.

TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said Trump's involvement in getting Jensen Huang’s old job back "looks terrible on its face." (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

And Trump’s intervention did not stop Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., from plowing ahead with a scheduled hearing with Huang. He announced that the embattled, newly reinstated CEO would appear before the panel on Dec. 3.

Gallego, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News Digital in a brief interview that "it really frightens me about what's happened with our national security," and questioned whether Trump had engaged "in stock market manipulation before making these announcements."

"All these things, you know, are really now up in the air," he said. "And at the core, the question is, what's going to happen to our national security?"

And Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has made AI safeguards a center of his challenge against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital that Huang was "at the center of this political corruption and political rot, and he seems to have been given a free hand by President Trump when it comes to formulating the Trump administration's AI and chips policy."

The lawmaker is also a member of the Banking Committee, and said he was keenly interested in Huang's "efforts to increase and accelerate the export of high-end chips to China, how he's been accomplishing that, how he's been getting his way with the administration."

"And then obviously, the concern is that it is undermining our national security interests. After all, high-end chips can be used by the military in China," Van Hollen said. "And it's completely it's just completely hypocritical for the Trump administration, on the one hand, to say the reason we have to take off all the brakes on AI development here at home is because China will leap ahead, if we don't, when in fact, it's the Trump administration that's helping China leap ahead."

Senate Republicans are equally uneasy about the national security implications of the move, despite Trump assuring in a post on Truth Social that "the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security."

"No national security risk? Based on what," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, said on X.

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., a member of the Senate Banking Committee, also told Fox News Digital that it was Nvidia’s right to reinstate Huang, but that the CEO needed to answer for what happened.

"Jensen Huang’s actions raised national security concerns, and he must answer for them," Britt said. "The Commerce Department also has a responsibility to explain the role it played in allowing for potentially serious threats to our national security."

"I look forward to having both Jensen Huang and Secretary Lutnick in front of the United States Senate Banking Committee, where my colleagues and I can ask questions and conduct necessary oversight," she continued.

The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is a great choice for beginners and experienced points-and-miles enthusiasts who want an easy way to earn miles — all for an affordable $95 annual fee.

The Venture Rewards card's current welcome offer is especially compelling — but this is your last chance to take advantage of it.

You can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening. Plus, you'll receive a $300 credit upon approval to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year.

Here's what the offer is worth and what to know before applying.

Apply now for a limited-time offer on the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card: Earn more than $1,000 in travel bonuses with a limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, plus earn 75,000 bonus miles once you spend $4,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

New Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening. Plus, you'll receive a $300 credit upon approval to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year. This offer ends soon.

Including the credit, this offer is worth $1,688, per TPG’s November 2026 valuations.

In terms of miles alone, this is the standard welcome bonus on the card. However, the inclusion of the $300 credit makes this offer among the most valuable we've seen.

For comparison, previous welcome offers have gone as high as 100,000 miles after meeting the minimum spending requirements (no longer available), but with no credit.

It’s possible to squeeze even more from that bonus if you redeem Capital One miles for maximum value, thanks to their impressive roster of 15-plus transfer partners.

There are some eligibility requirements to keep in mind before applying. You don't want to waste a hard pull on your credit report if you aren't eligible for the current offer.

First, if you've previously earned a welcome bonus on the Venture Rewards, you won't be able to earn another one for 48 months. Note that this is 48 months from the date you received your bonus, not from the date you were approved.

In addition, if you previously earned a welcome bonus on the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, you will more than likely not be eligible to earn a welcome bonus on the Venture Rewards.

Capital One may consider multiple factors when deciding whether to approve you; for a deeper dive into its application requirements, check out our full guide.

Related: The best Capital One credit cards

This card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on all purchases. So, by spending $4,000 on it to earn the welcome bonus, you’d earn at least 83,000 miles in the first few months, including the welcome bonus.

And since the Venture Rewards earns 5 miles per dollar spent on car rentals, hotels and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel, it’s possible to earn even more miles while working toward your welcome bonus.

While some travel credit cards may earn slightly higher rates on select categories such as groceries or dining, the draw here is the simplicity and guarantee of earning at least 2 miles per dollar spent on anything you buy without the need to memorize multiple bonus spending categories.

Related: Why I keep the Capital One Venture Rewards card in my wallet

When converting your miles to hotel points or airline miles, most partners offer a 1:1 transfer ratio, though a couple of partners have different ratios. You can get great sweet spot redemptions by transferring miles to programs like Air Canada Aeroplan and Air France-KLM Flying Blue.

For example, TPG's editor-in-chief, Nick Ewen, transferred 117,000 Capital One miles to Emirates Skywards to upgrade himself and two family members to Emirates first class. This broke down to 39,000 miles per person, a reasonable cost for the upgrade.

If you don’t want to transfer your miles, you can redeem them by booking a trip through Capital One Travel. These redemptions can be very handy in a world where you may be renting recreational vehicles, booking vacation home rentals or securing a cabin close to home more often than hopping on a flight to the other side of the world.

But for its modest $95 annual fee, the Venture Rewards provides some useful benefits:

The Capital One Venture Rewards remains a strong option for travelers who value simplicity. It earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases and gives cardholders access to Capital One's airline and hotel transfer partners, all for a $95 annual fee.

Plus, the current welcome offer — which ends soon — includes a solid haul of miles and a $300 credit for Capital One Travel, one of the best offers we've seen. Just remember to use your credit in the first cardholder year, or you'll forfeit the value.
