#6051. Marriott’s Worst Hotel? Rated 1.6 Stars On Its Own Site—A Guest Found Radisson Signs, Stained Sheets And A Filthy Sofa

Marriott’s Buena Park Grand Hotel & Suites promises “award-winning hospitality.” Guests rate it 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website. A reader checked in and found stained bedding and a sofa he wouldn’t sit on. I’ve written about the 1.7-star Woodlands Plaza Toledo Hotel as a contender for the worst Marriott in North America, and about the Carambola Beach Resort, Marriott’s “regret resort.” Apparently there’s more competition in the race to the bottom. Under Bill Marriott, Marriott’s sine qua non was consistency. They didn’t always promise a lot, but they delivered exactly what they promised. The point of booking a chain was knowing what you’d get. You didn’t need to investigate eeach property to find out whether it met basic standards. You knew what the brand stood for. Now I find Marriott overpromises and enforces too little, afraid of alienating owners by making them spend money. Net rooms growth has become the priority, even when the rooms undermine the reason customers choose Marriott in the first place. Here, the property isn’t even flying one of Marriott’s flags yet and presumably there will be some investment. But they aren’t making the owner do that first, before delivering their guests. They’re trading a reputation built over decades for current fee revenue. Owners pay Marriott to deliver customers. If travelers stop trusting the company’s hotels, Marriott has fewer customers to send those owners. Then the owners have little reason to keep paying Marriott. Letting bad hotels stay in the system earns fee revenue from those properties today but sacrifices the ability of the chain to earn anything in the future. The Buena Park property is expected to transition to SpringHill Suites. Here’s a guest review from a reader with Lifetime Titanium status, who found Marriott asking $144.37 for the night. He paid less through Delta’s hotel booking portal. This is what he found. Marriott wanted $140 for a 1.6-star hotel Marriott wanted $144.37 a night for the Grand Hotel & Suites in Buena Park, California, an unbranded property that guests had rated 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website. I booked it for less through Delta and found stains on the fitted sheet, red stains beneath a pillowcase and hair on a sofa I wouldn’t sit on.  When you book a Marriott, you expect a Marriott. The whole point of having a hotel company’s name behind a reservation is that somebody has exercised a little judgment on your behalf. What judgment did Marriott International exercise here?  The Grand is supposed to, at some point, become a SpringHill Suites by Marriott. When I arrived, I saw no Marriott signs. Some of the old signs and placards still said Radisson. I paid $125.22 through Delta Air Lines’ hotel booking portal. With the branding up in the air, I couldn’t tell what Bonvoy benefits or points I’d receive for paying $144.37 to book directly with Marriott. Priceline would have saved me $13.25 over Delta, but I’d have missed out on the nearly 600 SkyMiles I earned.  I arrived just after 2 p.m. The front desk clerk said my room was ready, but I’d have to pay $35 to check in before 3 p.m. I passed and came back a little more than an hour later. To be fair, I’d booked through a third party. Still, I gave the clerk my Bonvoy number at check-in. She never acknowledged my Lifetime Titanium Elite status or mentioned any benefits. I didn’t even get a bottle of water. The thing is, I liked the building. Its Spanish mission revival architecture was distinctive. You could also see where a restaurant and lounge had once been located. Whoever built the Grand clearly spent money on it. I suspect it was a great hotel in the early 1980s. More than four decades of neglect had, however, turned it into a dump. I booked a park-view suite with one king bed and one sofa bed. The view from my second-floor junior suite was of a parking lot and, beyond it, the main thoroughfare.  At first glance, the room looked clean. Apart from the flooring and the one TV, I’d guess it had been 20 years since anything had been updated. Even the laminate flooring was peeling and torn. The toiletries in the bathroom were a mix of brands. The tub and shower had extensive patches of what looked like black mold. Then I looked at the sofa. There was hair and debris on it. One reason to book a suite is to have somewhere to sit besides the bed. That left the bed, where I found what appeared to be fluid stains on the bedding, including the fitted sheet. Under one pillowcase, the pillow protector had red stains of its own. The Grand fell well short of what I’d expect from a Quality Inn or a Ramada. I’d put it at what I expect from the nearby Motel 6. At Marriott’s rate of $144.37, staying here is highway robbery. I don’t believe for a minute this property would have made it into the chain in this condition when the Marriott family ran the company. I can imagine Bill Marriott saying, “Call us when the renovations are finished.” Arne Sorenson, the first CEO from outside the Marriott family, and his successor, Tony Capuano, ruined the brand the Marriotts built. SpringHill Suites is supposed to be one of Marriott’s better limited-service brands. It will be a long time before the Grand comes anywhere close to that standard.  Topics on this pageBuena Park Grand Hotel & SuitesMarriott InternationalSpringHill SuitesAnthony CapuanoArne M. SorensonBill MarriottCaliforniaDelta Air LinesMarriott BonvoyMotel 6North AmericaPriceline.comRadisson HotelsRamada+11 more More From View from the Wing

I’ve written about the 1.7-star Woodlands Plaza Toledo Hotel as a contender for the worst Marriott in North America, and about the Carambola Beach Resort, Marriott’s “regret resort.” Apparently there’s more competition in the race to the bottom.

Under Bill Marriott, Marriott’s sine qua non was consistency. They didn’t always promise a lot, but they delivered exactly what they promised. The point of booking a chain was knowing what you’d get. You didn’t need to investigate eeach property to find out whether it met basic standards. You knew what the brand stood for.

Now I find Marriott overpromises and enforces too little, afraid of alienating owners by making them spend money. Net rooms growth has become the priority, even when the rooms undermine the reason customers choose Marriott in the first place. Here, the property isn’t even flying one of Marriott’s flags yet and presumably there will be some investment. But they aren’t making the owner do that first, before delivering their guests.

They’re trading a reputation built over decades for current fee revenue. Owners pay Marriott to deliver customers. If travelers stop trusting the company’s hotels, Marriott has fewer customers to send those owners. Then the owners have little reason to keep paying Marriott. Letting bad hotels stay in the system earns fee revenue from those properties today but sacrifices the ability of the chain to earn anything in the future.

The Buena Park property is expected to transition to SpringHill Suites. Here’s a guest review from a reader with Lifetime Titanium status, who found Marriott asking $144.37 for the night. He paid less through Delta’s hotel booking portal. This is what he found.

Marriott wanted $140 for a 1.6-star hotel

Marriott wanted $144.37 a night for the Grand Hotel & Suites in Buena Park, California, an unbranded property that guests had rated 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website.

I booked it for less through Delta and found stains on the fitted sheet, red stains beneath a pillowcase and hair on a sofa I wouldn’t sit on.

When you book a Marriott, you expect a Marriott. The whole point of having a hotel company’s name behind a reservation is that somebody has exercised a little judgment on your behalf. What judgment did Marriott International exercise here?

The Grand is supposed to, at some point, become a SpringHill Suites by Marriott. When I arrived, I saw no Marriott signs. Some of the old signs and placards still said Radisson.

I paid $125.22 through Delta Air Lines’ hotel booking portal. With the branding up in the air, I couldn’t tell what Bonvoy benefits or points I’d receive for paying $144.37 to book directly with Marriott. Priceline would have saved me $13.25 over Delta, but I’d have missed out on the nearly 600 SkyMiles I earned.

I arrived just after 2 p.m. The front desk clerk said my room was ready, but I’d have to pay $35 to check in before 3 p.m. I passed and came back a little more than an hour later.

To be fair, I’d booked through a third party. Still, I gave the clerk my Bonvoy number at check-in. She never acknowledged my Lifetime Titanium Elite status or mentioned any benefits. I didn’t even get a bottle of water.

The thing is, I liked the building. Its Spanish mission revival architecture was distinctive. You could also see where a restaurant and lounge had once been located. Whoever built the Grand clearly spent money on it. I suspect it was a great hotel in the early 1980s. More than four decades of neglect had, however, turned it into a dump.

I booked a park-view suite with one king bed and one sofa bed. The view from my second-floor junior suite was of a parking lot and, beyond it, the main thoroughfare.

At first glance, the room looked clean. Apart from the flooring and the one TV, I’d guess it had been 20 years since anything had been updated. Even the laminate flooring was peeling and torn. The toiletries in the bathroom were a mix of brands. The tub and shower had extensive patches of what looked like black mold.

Then I looked at the sofa. There was hair and debris on it. One reason to book a suite is to have somewhere to sit besides the bed. That left the bed, where I found what appeared to be fluid stains on the bedding, including the fitted sheet. Under one pillowcase, the pillow protector had red stains of its own.

The Grand fell well short of what I’d expect from a Quality Inn or a Ramada. I’d put it at what I expect from the nearby Motel 6. At Marriott’s rate of $144.37, staying here is highway robbery.

I don’t believe for a minute this property would have made it into the chain in this condition when the Marriott family ran the company. I can imagine Bill Marriott saying, “Call us when the renovations are finished.”

Arne Sorenson, the first CEO from outside the Marriott family, and his successor, Tony Capuano, ruined the brand the Marriotts built.

SpringHill Suites is supposed to be one of Marriott’s better limited-service brands. It will be a long time before the Grand comes anywhere close to that standard.

#6049. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

#6048. Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select Review—Why American Still Wins For Credit Card Spending Toward Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

American Airlines has the best overall U.S. program for making credit card spending count toward status, and you don’t need one of its expensive premium cards to take advantage of it.

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] earns one Loyalty Point per eligible dollar, without a cap. You can combine those points with what you earn flying, shopping and through many of American’s other partners, all the way up to Executive Platinum. Meanwhile, the card’s checked bag benefit can cover its annual fee on a single family trip.

I recently covered the card’s refresh, which adds Walmart+, an inflight credit and travel protections while raising the annual fee. Those changes take effect January 24, 2027. They improve the card for some customers, but the reason to put spending on it remains earning status.

American’s current offer is 50,000 bonus miles after $2,500 in purchases within the first three months. There’s no annual fee for the first 12 months then $99, increasing to $150 with renewals starting January 24, 2027. That means for new applications, after the introductory year, the card’s annual fee is $150. Citi’s initial bonus restriction looks back 48 months. You aren’t eligible if you’ve received a Platinum Select new account bonus during that period, or converted another Citi card on which you earned a new account bonus during that period into a Platinum Select. A bonus on a different American Airlines card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The miles are worth having. I’ve written about American’s partner award sweet spots, like 70,000 miles for business class between North America and the Middle East or Indian Subcontinent. And I find the miles useful for domestic travel too, often uncovering good mileage deals when cash prices are high (my sense that American doesn’t want to discount the fare, but doesn’t expect to fill the plane without doing so). Why American Is Best Overall For Spending Toward Status The card earns one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible purchases. There’s no annual cap on that earning and no minimum flight requirement to qualify for American’s published status levels. Here are the thresholds, and the spending that would reach them if you earned nothing from flights, partners or separate Loyalty Point bonuses: AAdvantage Status   Loyalty Points   Card Spending Alone Gold   40,000   $40,000 Platinum   75,000   $75,000 Platinum Pro   125,000   $125,000 Executive Platinum   200,000   $200,000 American’s qualification year runs March 1 through the last day of February.If flights and other activity get you to 110,000 Loyalty Points, another $15,000 in eligible card purchases gets you to Platinum Pro. You can fill the gap with expenses you were going to incur anyway. The same Loyalty Points also move you toward Loyalty Point Rewards, including opportunities to select systemwide upgrades. Compare this with the UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees), which earns one Premier qualifying point per $20 and caps that earning at 1,000 points annually. That’s only part of the 6,000 points needed for United’s points-based Silver qualification path, which also requires at least four United or United Express flights. The similarly priced Platinum Select can take you all the way to American’s top published tier. Even Delta’s premium Reserve card takes $255,000 in purchases to earn Diamond through spending plus that one card’s annual head start. That’s 28,000 qualifying dollars, less the card’s 2,500-dollar head start, earned at one qualifying dollar per $10 spent. American’s $200,000 Executive Platinum threshold is available on this much less expensive card. Alaska’s Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card ($395 annual fee) earns one status point per $2, without a cap, plus 10,000 status points annually beginning with the first anniversary. It can require less spending for particular tiers. American is my overall pick because of the combination of inexpensive cards, uncapped earning, and the ability to combine spending with so many other sources of status credit. What You Earn On Purchases The January refresh expands the bonus categories: Eligible Purchases   Today   From January 24, 2027 American Airlines, restaurants and gas stations   2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings through their respective sites   1 mile per dollar   3 miles per dollar Electric vehicle charging, select streaming services, and eligible rides and rail purchases   1 mile per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar Two miles per dollar on American Airlines tickets still doesn’t impress me. The Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) earns three points per dollar on airfare, hotels, restaurants, supermarkets, gas and electric vehicle charging. Its points transfer to American, and its annual fee is $95. If I just wanted redeemable American miles, I’d generally prefer Strata Premier for those categories. The value in spending on this card is progress towards AAdvantage status. Free Checked Bags Can Pay For The Card The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation get their first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries. American currently charges $45 online or $50 at the airport for the first checked bag on a standard domestic ticket. Basic economy costs $5 more. For two people each checking one bag on a domestic roundtrip, the savings are $180 compared with paying the standard fee online. That’s already more than the coming $150 annual fee. A family of four doing the same saves $360. You don’t have to buy the tickets with this card to receive the bag benefit. Your AAdvantage number needs to be on the reservation. The whole itinerary must qualify as domestic American Airlines or American Eagle travel. The primary cardmember must travel. An authorized user doesn’t get an independent bag allowance when traveling alone. If your status or cabin already includes a free bag, holding the card doesn’t add another one. You also get Group 5 preferred boarding, including up to four companions on the same reservation. That puts you ahead of later economy groups and improves your chances of finding overhead bin space. There are no foreign transaction fees, and authorized users can be added without an additional annual fee. Their spending earns miles and Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. Holding an eligible AAdvantage card also keeps the miles in the primary cardmember’s account from expiring. What The January Refresh Adds The annual fee rises $51. Key incremental benefits are: Walmart+ annual membership. The primary cardmember gets the $98 annual plan, including delivery benefits, fuel savings and a streaming choice. Someone already paying for it can come out ahead from this benefit alone. Up to $100 in annual inflight credits. Eligible food, drinks and Wi-Fi purchases qualify; Admirals Club purchases don’t. This replaces the existing 25% food and beverage rebate. Half off an annual FOX One subscription. I’d assign this value only if it’s something you already want to buy. The inflight credit is better than the old rebate for someone making a modest amount of purchases. Spend $100 on eligible food and drinks and you’d receive $100 back instead of $25. The added travel protections may be more useful than the subscription benefits. Trip delay: Up to $500 per covered traveler for eligible expenses after a covered delay of at least six hours. Paying just the taxes on an AAdvantage award doesn’t limit reimbursement to that small cash payment. Trip cancellation and interruption: Coverage is limited to the lesser of $5,000 per trip or the covered amount paid with the card and/or AAdvantage miles. Lost baggage: Up to $3,000 per covered traveler, with a $10,000 total per trip; a lower per-bag limit applies to New York residents. Rental cars: Up to $75,000 for covered damage, for eligible rentals up to 31 days. Coverage is secondary in the U.S. and primary outside it. These protections begin with the refresh. Required payment methods and covered reasons differ by benefit. The card also retains up to $180 in Turo credits per calendar year, limited to $30 per eligible completed trip. You need six rentals to use the full amount, must link the card to your Turo account, and need to pay directly with it rather than through a digital wallet. There’s also 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. The $20,000 Spending Bonus Is Useful, But Do The Math Currently, spending $20,000 during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150. The new discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after issue and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year. I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee. Which American Airlines Card Should You Have? Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. For someone who already has status, or another American Airlines card, I’d compare these options: Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] The $350 annual fee buys four Admirals Club Globe passes each calendar year, among other benefits. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee. The January refresh expands the bonus categories:

Two miles per dollar on American Airlines tickets still doesn’t impress me. The Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) earns three points per dollar on airfare, hotels, restaurants, supermarkets, gas and electric vehicle charging. Its points transfer to American, and its annual fee is $95.

If I just wanted redeemable American miles, I’d generally prefer Strata Premier for those categories. The value in spending on this card is progress towards AAdvantage status.

The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation get their first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries. American currently charges $45 online or $50 at the airport for the first checked bag on a standard domestic ticket. Basic economy costs $5 more. For two people each checking one bag on a domestic roundtrip, the savings are $180 compared with paying the standard fee online. That’s already more than the coming $150 annual fee. A family of four doing the same saves $360. You don’t have to buy the tickets with this card to receive the bag benefit. Your AAdvantage number needs to be on the reservation. The whole itinerary must qualify as domestic American Airlines or American Eagle travel. The primary cardmember must travel. An authorized user doesn’t get an independent bag allowance when traveling alone. If your status or cabin already includes a free bag, holding the card doesn’t add another one. You also get Group 5 preferred boarding, including up to four companions on the same reservation. That puts you ahead of later economy groups and improves your chances of finding overhead bin space. There are no foreign transaction fees, and authorized users can be added without an additional annual fee. Their spending earns miles and Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. Holding an eligible AAdvantage card also keeps the miles in the primary cardmember’s account from expiring. What The January Refresh Adds The annual fee rises $51. Key incremental benefits are: Walmart+ annual membership. The primary cardmember gets the $98 annual plan, including delivery benefits, fuel savings and a streaming choice. Someone already paying for it can come out ahead from this benefit alone. Up to $100 in annual inflight credits. Eligible food, drinks and Wi-Fi purchases qualify; Admirals Club purchases don’t. This replaces the existing 25% food and beverage rebate. Half off an annual FOX One subscription. I’d assign this value only if it’s something you already want to buy. The inflight credit is better than the old rebate for someone making a modest amount of purchases. Spend $100 on eligible food and drinks and you’d receive $100 back instead of $25. The added travel protections may be more useful than the subscription benefits. Trip delay: Up to $500 per covered traveler for eligible expenses after a covered delay of at least six hours. Paying just the taxes on an AAdvantage award doesn’t limit reimbursement to that small cash payment. Trip cancellation and interruption: Coverage is limited to the lesser of $5,000 per trip or the covered amount paid with the card and/or AAdvantage miles. Lost baggage: Up to $3,000 per covered traveler, with a $10,000 total per trip; a lower per-bag limit applies to New York residents. Rental cars: Up to $75,000 for covered damage, for eligible rentals up to 31 days. Coverage is secondary in the U.S. and primary outside it. These protections begin with the refresh. Required payment methods and covered reasons differ by benefit. The card also retains up to $180 in Turo credits per calendar year, limited to $30 per eligible completed trip. You need six rentals to use the full amount, must link the card to your Turo account, and need to pay directly with it rather than through a digital wallet. There’s also 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. The $20,000 Spending Bonus Is Useful, But Do The Math Currently, spending $20,000 during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150. The new discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after issue and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year. I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee. Which American Airlines Card Should You Have? Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. For someone who already has status, or another American Airlines card, I’d compare these options: Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] The $350 annual fee buys four Admirals Club Globe passes each calendar year, among other benefits. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee. #6046. First Look Inside American Airlines’ New Austin Lounge—Twice The Space, An Outdoor Terrace And Skyline Views

I finally got inside American Airlines’ new Austin airport lounge this week. It’s still a shell, but the covered outdoor terrace is already there, and you can see the downtown skyline from the west end of the lounge. The new Admirals Club will have more than twice the space of the current one, and Austin is just one of the places where American is building bigger lounges. American Airlines should be opening its New York JFK ‘Provisions’ grab ‘n go lounge for Admirals Club members in the next month, complete with barista bar. And we’ll see both the renovated Washington National D concourse and replacement Chicago O’Hare L concourse clubs next year. By the end of next year we should also see the new Austin Admiral’s Club as well. The core and shell space is about to be turned over to American by the airport, allowing them to begin construction work. The current club is small. It was perfect-sized when I moved to Austin, but Austin has grown and overall American Airlines lounge visits have increased 80% over the past decade. Expectations for food have increased, too, and the kitchen facilities are inadequate. American is replacing its current club with a new one at the west end of the airport’s main concourse. In March, American Airlines announced the details of the plan for the new club above gate 35. More than 12,000 square feet (more than double the size of the current club) With an outdoor terrace and views of both downtown and airport operations. Supporting a gate allocation that’s expected to nearly double when the new terminal opens in the early 2030s. I keep looking at the space, waiting for progress, each time I fly out of the airport. I’m anxious for the new lounge! So far there are two renderings of the space that have been made available: Credit: American Airlines Credit: American Airlines This week I had a chance to peek inside the space, see the actual views from the space and the outdoor terrace. When you come up the elevator or walk up the stairs you’ll see the entrance – they’ll be taking down a preexisting wall there, and will install e-gates which are a new club standard (like at the Philadelphia A-West club – that location also has e-gates for the Flagship business class lounge, but that won’t be a standard). The kitchen will be at the far left, back of the lounge when you enter. The full kitchen facilities will allow in-house preparation for upgraded food. Closer, also to the left but nearer the windows will be the bar. At the opposite (west) end of the lounge, you can see out towards the downtown skyline. It gives some perspective on how small Austin’s downtown really is, though it’s far more dense than it was when I first moved here. The lounge’s outdoor deck has covering and shade, and American tells me it will have misters and fans – making it much more usable throughout the year. Living in Austin we eat outdoors much of the year, though the summers can get very hot and there will be days you don’t want to be outdoors between November and February. The former Chase Terrace on the opposite end of the airport lacked covering and climate assistance. Taking photos from the lounge is a bit challenging, because of the screens that the airport installs on the window meant for birds to be able to identify the glass and not fly into the building. Nonetheless, angle the lens just right and zoom past it and your photos can come closer to what you see out the windows (you really don’t see these screens except when you’re up close to the glass). American’s Austin gate allocation goes from 4 to 9 — a 125% increase – when the new concourse opens in the early 2030s. American can use common use gates in addition today. All nine of their dedicated gates will be on the current concourse, near this new lounge. Austin is part of a larger investment American is now making in its clubs. After several years where there wasn’t any growth in its network, and they even closed some lounges, here’s the American Airlines lounge pipeline: Airport Project Timing / status Austin New Admirals Club above the west gate expansion: more than 12,000 square feet, roughly double the current club, with an outdoor terrace. Permits issued, but American hasn’t announced an opening date. Expected at the end of 2027. Charlotte New Admirals Club above the airport atrium: more than 40,000 square feet, with showers, multiple bars and food stations. 2028 anticipated. Charlotte First Flagship Lounge, separately announced from the new Admirals Club. Size and opening date haven’t been disclosed. Chicago O’Hare Replacement Concourse L Admirals Club exceeding 10,000 square feet, with more seating and airfield views. Construction underway. Existing L club stays open during the work. No opening date announced. Dallas–Fort Worth New Terminal C Admirals Club: 37,000 square feet near the Skylink station. No opening date disclosed. Dallas–Fort Worth Terminal F Provisions by Admirals Club, the initial lounge offering in a broader premium-space program for the new terminal. Planned for Terminal F’s first phase. Later premium spaces and individual opening dates haven’t been shared. Miami New Flagship Lounge and expanded D30 Admirals Club. The current Flagship space becomes Admirals Club space, nearly doubling American’s total lounge footprint at the airport. No opening date disclosed. Nashville Replacement Admirals Club in the new Concourse A: about 17,400 square feet including outdoor terraces and an interior balcony, replacing the current roughly 7,000 square foot club. Construction expected to begin in 2027. No firm opening date announced. New York JFK Provisions by Admirals Club in Terminal 8: 3,700 square feet near gates 12–14, with hot and cold food, a dedicated barista bar and customer assistance. Targeted for December 2026. Phoenix Expansion and refresh of all three Terminal 4 Admirals Clubs. Near term work at A19–A21 improves food service. The B5–B7 club gets 20% more seats. Longer term, the two A clubs nearly triple their combined space and add approximately 150% more seats. Announced November 2026. No completion dates disclosed. San Antonio First Admirals Club in new Terminal C. Airport plans specify a 10,000 square foot American Airlines lounge. Documented by the airport, no formal American lounge announcement yet. Terminal C targets mid-2028, but no separate lounge opening date. Washington National Rebuilt Concourse D Admirals Club: more than 10,000 square feet and approximately 50% more seats. Expected to deliver in 2027. The real treat in Austin, though, isn’t the design or that there will be an outdoor deck – it’s the staff in the Austin club who are the absolute best in the system. They know the names of all regulars on sight and welcome you into the lounge. They work magic with itineraries – and they keep working that magic even once you’ve left, frequently bird dogging inventory and improving connections even after you’ve left the lounge. When I’ve had flights cancelled and could only get a long connection in Dallas or Charlotte, I’ve found myself landing to notes saying they’ve gotten me on an earlier flight because space opened up. They do this for everyone. It’s a small city, personal customer service feel even in a growing market. And that makes Admirals Club membership (and Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] cardmembership) worth it. The Austin club space will finally match the service once this lounge opens. I genuinely cannot wait for the lounge to open because it’ll make flying American Airlines out of my home airport that much better. By the end of next year we should also see the new Austin Admiral’s Club as well. The core and shell space is about to be turned over to American by the airport, allowing them to begin construction work.

The current club is small. It was perfect-sized when I moved to Austin, but Austin has grown and overall American Airlines lounge visits have increased 80% over the past decade. Expectations for food have increased, too, and the kitchen facilities are inadequate. American is replacing its current club with a new one at the west end of the airport’s main concourse.

In March, American Airlines announced the details of the plan for the new club above gate 35.

More than 12,000 square feet (more than double the size of the current club) With an outdoor terrace and views of both downtown and airport operations. Supporting a gate allocation that’s expected to nearly double when the new terminal opens in the early 2030s. I keep looking at the space, waiting for progress, each time I fly out of the airport. I’m anxious for the new lounge! So far there are two renderings of the space that have been made available: Credit: American Airlines Credit: American Airlines This week I had a chance to peek inside the space, see the actual views from the space and the outdoor terrace. When you come up the elevator or walk up the stairs you’ll see the entrance – they’ll be taking down a preexisting wall there, and will install e-gates which are a new club standard (like at the Philadelphia A-West club – that location also has e-gates for the Flagship business class lounge, but that won’t be a standard). The kitchen will be at the far left, back of the lounge when you enter. The full kitchen facilities will allow in-house preparation for upgraded food. Closer, also to the left but nearer the windows will be the bar. At the opposite (west) end of the lounge, you can see out towards the downtown skyline. It gives some perspective on how small Austin’s downtown really is, though it’s far more dense than it was when I first moved here. The lounge’s outdoor deck has covering and shade, and American tells me it will have misters and fans – making it much more usable throughout the year. Living in Austin we eat outdoors much of the year, though the summers can get very hot and there will be days you don’t want to be outdoors between November and February. The former Chase Terrace on the opposite end of the airport lacked covering and climate assistance. Taking photos from the lounge is a bit challenging, because of the screens that the airport installs on the window meant for birds to be able to identify the glass and not fly into the building. Nonetheless, angle the lens just right and zoom past it and your photos can come closer to what you see out the windows (you really don’t see these screens except when you’re up close to the glass). American’s Austin gate allocation goes from 4 to 9 — a 125% increase – when the new concourse opens in the early 2030s. American can use common use gates in addition today. All nine of their dedicated gates will be on the current concourse, near this new lounge. Austin is part of a larger investment American is now making in its clubs. After several years where there wasn’t any growth in its network, and they even closed some lounges, here’s the American Airlines lounge pipeline: Airport Project Timing / status Austin New Admirals Club above the west gate expansion: more than 12,000 square feet, roughly double the current club, with an outdoor terrace. Permits issued, but American hasn’t announced an opening date. Expected at the end of 2027. Charlotte New Admirals Club above the airport atrium: more than 40,000 square feet, with showers, multiple bars and food stations. 2028 anticipated. Charlotte First Flagship Lounge, separately announced from the new Admirals Club. Size and opening date haven’t been disclosed. Chicago O’Hare Replacement Concourse L Admirals Club exceeding 10,000 square feet, with more seating and airfield views. Construction underway. Existing L club stays open during the work. No opening date announced. Dallas–Fort Worth New Terminal C Admirals Club: 37,000 square feet near the Skylink station. No opening date disclosed. Dallas–Fort Worth Terminal F Provisions by Admirals Club, the initial lounge offering in a broader premium-space program for the new terminal. Planned for Terminal F’s first phase. Later premium spaces and individual opening dates haven’t been shared. Miami New Flagship Lounge and expanded D30 Admirals Club. The current Flagship space becomes Admirals Club space, nearly doubling American’s total lounge footprint at the airport. No opening date disclosed. Nashville Replacement Admirals Club in the new Concourse A: about 17,400 square feet including outdoor terraces and an interior balcony, replacing the current roughly 7,000 square foot club. Construction expected to begin in 2027. No firm opening date announced. New York JFK Provisions by Admirals Club in Terminal 8: 3,700 square feet near gates 12–14, with hot and cold food, a dedicated barista bar and customer assistance. Targeted for December 2026. Phoenix Expansion and refresh of all three Terminal 4 Admirals Clubs. Near term work at A19–A21 improves food service. The B5–B7 club gets 20% more seats. Longer term, the two A clubs nearly triple their combined space and add approximately 150% more seats. Announced November 2026. No completion dates disclosed. San Antonio First Admirals Club in new Terminal C. Airport plans specify a 10,000 square foot American Airlines lounge. Documented by the airport, no formal American lounge announcement yet. Terminal C targets mid-2028, but no separate lounge opening date. Washington National Rebuilt Concourse D Admirals Club: more than 10,000 square feet and approximately 50% more seats. Expected to deliver in 2027. The real treat in Austin, though, isn’t the design or that there will be an outdoor deck – it’s the staff in the Austin club who are the absolute best in the system. They know the names of all regulars on sight and welcome you into the lounge. They work magic with itineraries – and they keep working that magic even once you’ve left, frequently bird dogging inventory and improving connections even after you’ve left the lounge. When I’ve had flights cancelled and could only get a long connection in Dallas or Charlotte, I’ve found myself landing to notes saying they’ve gotten me on an earlier flight because space opened up. They do this for everyone. It’s a small city, personal customer service feel even in a growing market. And that makes Admirals Club membership (and Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] cardmembership) worth it. The Austin club space will finally match the service once this lounge opens. I genuinely cannot wait for the lounge to open because it’ll make flying American Airlines out of my home airport that much better. #6045. Ryanair Flew 208 Million Passengers At An Average Fare Of $56—Now Its Rivals Want It Grounded For Not Being European Enough

A trade group representing Lufthansa, Air France and KLM has gone to court in Ireland to challenge Ryanair’s right to fly. Their objection is to who owns the airline that carried 208 million passengers at an average fare of just €51 in the year ended March 31. European investors hold just 30% of Ryanair’s shares. Competitors say they run afoul of foreign ownership rules, but those European investors exercise 100% voting control of the ariline. I don’t see Europe grounding Ryanair. I do see why its competitors might like want to pick this fight. The European Network Airlines Association says it asked the European Commission and national regulators to check Ryanair’s ownership after the airline loosened its share purchase rules. That didn’t get them what they wanted so they sued the Irish Aviation Authority. On November 16, the judge declined to add Lufthansa, Air France and KLM as parties to the case, though they can submit affidavits. A hearing is scheduled for December 16. Who Owns Ryanair, And Who Gets Control? Brexit turned British shareholders into foreign investors without anybody having to sell a share. Since January 2021, nonqualifying shareholders haven’t been allowed to attend, speak or vote at Ryanair shareholder meetings. On March 7, 2025, Ryanair let them buy ordinary shares in Dublin again. It kept the voting ban, including for any votes the chairman might otherwise cast on their behalf. Ryanair says the change opened the door to inclusion in stock indexes. Its board said it would restrict purchases again if European ownership fell to 20%. . At both March 31 and September 30 this year, Ryanair put qualifying European ownership at 30%. That includes investors from Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. Shares held through its U.S. depositary are generally non-qualifying. Here’s who shows up in Ryanair’s March 31 shareholder disclosure. Reported holder    Share of Ryanair Capital Group 14.6% MFS 4.7% Artisan Partners 4.5% Michael O’Leary 4.0% BlackRock 4.0% Fidelity 3.3% By October, Capital Group reported 15.70% for client accounts, and T. Rowe Price reported 3.00%. O’Leary’s 4% economic stake translates to 13% voting control. Does It Matter More Who Owns The Shares Or Who Controls The Airline? European law requires both. Qualifying states or their nationals have to own more than half the airline and effectively control it. Giving Europeans every vote solves the legal issue of control. The key legal question here is whether shares that carry no voting rights count as equity for the ownership test. European regulators have allowed this in the past. Wizz Air says British and Hungarian regulators approved its plan to suspend some foreign shareholders’ votes after Brexit so Wizz Air Hungary could keep its European license. easyJet just did this in a takeover vote. When shareholders approved an Apollo deal on November 11, qualifying Europeans owned 35.07% of easyJet. It suspended voting rights on 233,921,894 shares. Those shareholders keep their dividend rights. The proposed deal itself caps Apollo’s ordinary equity at 49.9%. But this is complicated. A 1995 Swissair–Sabena decision found that Swissair held 49.5% of the Belgian airline’s voting shares, plus special certificates that the European Commission agreed to leave out of the ownership calculation. Those certificates had no votes, generally paid at least 5% and gave Swissair no share of the assets left over in liquidation. That looked like debt. In contrast, a Ryanair shareholder who can’t vote still collects dividends (which aren’t fixed) and gains or loses money on fluctuations of the stock. What Happens If Ryanair Loses? If all the ordinary shares count, Ryanair has to get qualifying ownership above 50%. That’s 207 million existing shares moving from non-European to European owners (assuming they don’t issue new shares). The airline’s articles of incorporation allow it to direct restricted holders to sell to qualifying investors. This is being framed in some quarters as Ryanair having to shut down. That doesn’t seem likely. I’ve been writing about foreign airline ownership since 2003. If someone abroad is willing to put up the money for more planes and cheaper flights, what does the passenger gain by turning them away? If Europe needs aircraft and crews available for defense, it can pay airlines to provide them. Forcing a British retiree to sell Ryanair stock to a Frenchman doesn’t add aircraft that Europe can use for its defense. It does, however, give Lufthansa and Air France a way to raise a competitor’s cost of capital. So it’s decent return on trade association dues. There is a lot to love about JetBlue. The airline offers generous legroom, tasty snacks and free Wi-Fi. It also has a fairly straightforward loyalty program.

JetBlue TrueBlue points are easy to earn through flights, partner activity, cobranded credit cards and transferable rewards. They are also easy to redeem because any seat on a JetBlue-operated flight can be booked with points, and there are no blackout dates. The program has become more useful through an expanding network of airline partners, including the Blue Sky partnership with United Airlines.

Here is everything you need to know about the JetBlue TrueBlue loyalty program.

JetBlue serves more than 100 destinations throughout the U.S., Latin America, Canada, the Caribbean and Europe. The airline isn’t part of any global alliance but has a growing roster of airline partners.

With JetBlue being one of the youngest major airlines in the U.S., the TrueBlue loyalty program is a relative newcomer to the points and miles world. The program is revenue-based, so earning and redeeming points are typically tied to ticket prices. However, there are also many ways to earn JetBlue points without even getting on an airplane.

TrueBlue points do not expire. Points Pooling also lets between two and seven friends or family members combine their balances, although members must contribute all of their points to the pool while participating.

Related: How to change or cancel a JetBlue flight

JetBlue isn't part of a global alliance, but TrueBlue members can earn and redeem points with the following airline partners.

JetBlue says earning and redeeming with Cape Air are temporarily unavailable while it updates its systems.

Blue Sky lets TrueBlue members earn points and Tiles on eligible United-operated flights booked through JetBlue and redeem TrueBlue points for United flights through JetBlue. Mosaic members also receive reciprocal perks on United, including priority boarding, one complimentary checked bag, preferred seating and Economy Plus seats at check-in. Base fares receive the above benefits except seat selection, and the partnership does not provide reciprocal lounge access.

You can join TrueBlue for free online, starting at the “basic” level. The four published tiers of JetBlue elite status are:

JetBlue uses Tiles to track progress toward "Perks You Pick" — a selection of benefits you can choose from after earning a set number of Tiles — and Mosaic status. You earn 1 Tile for every:

Government-imposed taxes, government-imposed fees and travel insurance do not earn Tiles. Tiles are a status metric and cannot be redeemed for travel.

This means you could earn elite status entirely through credit card spending, through qualifying travel spending or with a combination of the two.

Before reaching Mosaic 1, members can choose a different Perks You Pick benefit at 10, 20, 30 and 40 Tiles. Through Jan. 31, 2027, the choices include early boarding, priority security, a complimentary first inflight alcoholic drink, double points per dollar spent on a JetBlue Vacations package or 5,000 bonus points.

You can pick each of these only once, even if you earn all four Tile amounts.

Related: JetBlue changes its boarding order with new groups

Mosaic members also choose one Perks You Pick benefit at each status level. Current choices include a pet fee waiver, IHG One Rewards Platinum Elite status, Mint Suite selection priority, FoundersCard Blue membership, a $99 statement credit for an eligible JetBlue credit card, a 20-Tile bonus for the member or another TrueBlue member and 15,000 bonus points.

Changes are coming in 2027: Beginning Feb. 1, members will receive a new tier-specific Perks You Pick menu at each Mosaic milestone, may select the same perk again at a later milestone and will have 60 days to make each choice. A pet fee waiver will become an automatic Mosaic 2 benefit, while eligible JetBlue Premier Card members will gain additional card-exclusive choices.

The information for the JetBlue Premier Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Separately, when BlueFirst service begins Dec. 8, all Mosaic members and one companion on the same reservation will be eligible for complimentary, space-available upgrades on eligible BlueFirst flights. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares will not be eligible.

Related: JetBlue announces first-class upgrades and new elite benefits for 2027

There are many ways to save up for a JetBlue award ticket.

When flying JetBlue, you’ll earn TrueBlue points based on the ticket cost, the fare type and whether you book directly with JetBlue.

JetBlue now sells Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst and Mint experiences, with Base and Flex variants available in most cabins. Base fares earn 1 base point per dollar spent, plus 1 point per dollar when booked on jetblue.com or through the JetBlue app. Standard and Flex fares earn 3 base points per dollar spent, plus 3 points per dollar when booked directly.

You can earn TrueBlue points on eligible flights operated by United Airlines, Condor, Etihad Airways, Icelandair, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines and South African Airways.

United is different from JetBlue's other partners. TrueBlue members earn 5 points per dollar spent on eligible United-operated flights booked through JetBlue; government-imposed taxes, fees and surcharges are excluded. Eligible United flights credited to TrueBlue also earn Tiles. For most other partners, earning depends on the operating airline, the booking class and the distance flown.

You can find each partner’s earning chart in JetBlue’s partner directory.

There are several ways to earn TrueBlue points without flying:

You can also purchase JetBlue points or pool them with other members.

JetBlue also offers Points On Repeat subscriptions. These provide a set number of TrueBlue points each month. Higher tiers add a flight-earning accelerator, while the top tier also includes a 10% rebate on eligible JetBlue award flights. Compare the subscription cost with the value you expect to receive before enrolling.

JetBlue has four cobranded credit cards, all issued by Barclays:

The information for the JetBlue Premier Card, the JetBlue Plus Card, the JetBlue Card and the JetBlue Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

TrueBlue is also a transfer partner of seven flexible rewards currencies at the following transfer rates:

Related: Credit card transfer partners: Guide to transferring points and miles to airlines and hotels

JetBlue uses a dynamic pricing scheme for its own flights, so redemptions are pretty straightforward. You can redeem points for any seat on any JetBlue-operated flight across its entire route network. The more a flight costs in cash, the more it will cost in points.

According to TPG’s November 2026 valuations, TrueBlue points are worth 1.35 cents each on average. To calculate the value of a specific award, subtract any taxes and fees from the cash price, divide the result by the number of points required and multiply by 100. Mint and Cash + Points bookings may offer less value, while some partner awards can offer more.

To check award availability, search for flights on JetBlue’s website as you normally would and check the “Use TrueBlue points” option at the top of the search box. Base fares can now be booked with points, although JetBlue charges $150 per person to change or cancel a Base award.

Cash + Points bookings start at 500 points and are available for JetBlue-operated flights and eligible JetBlue Vacations packages. This option can be useful if you are short on points, but it often delivers less value than a standard award. Cash + Points bookings are not available for partner airline awards.

TrueBlue points can also cover certain seat assignments, checked bags, pet fees and priority security. You can redeem points through TrueBlue Travel for eligible hotel stays and car rentals as well.

In addition to using your points for JetBlue flights, you can redeem TrueBlue points on JetBlue's site for eligible flights operated by United Airlines, Condor, Etihad Airways, Icelandair, Qatar Airways and China Airlines. Cape Air redemptions are temporarily paused.

Partner award availability can be limited, and each one-way award must be operated by a single carrier. Frustratingly, you cannot combine a JetBlue flight and a partner flight on the same one-way award, although you can book the outbound and return on different airlines.

A Points Pooling account can have two to seven members and must include at least one person age 21 or older. Members contribute 100% of the points they earn after joining. The pool leader and anyone granted redemption privileges can use pooled points without the other members' permission, so only pool with people you trust. A member who leaves takes their remaining points balance with them.

Related: Family points pooling: How to transfer and maximize your rewards

While you’re unlikely to get incredible value from your points, the JetBlue TrueBlue program is still useful for many travelers. TrueBlue points are among the easiest domestic airline points to earn and redeem. JetBlue-operated awards do not require an award chart and have no blackout dates, though partner award availability can be restricted.

JetBlue's expanded partner network makes TrueBlue more globally useful. New transfer partnerships with Rove and Bilt also make it easier to top up a balance. JetBlue's revenue-based pricing usually limits the opportunity for exceptional value on its own flights, but straightforward redemptions and occasional high-value partner awards make TrueBlue worth understanding.

#6043. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#6042. Dems brush off Elon Musk's anti-MAGA pivot, warn DOGE probe still coming

Democratic lawmakers react to Elon Musk saying he’s "not MAGA," speaking on his role in DOGE, potential investigations and whether they could work with him. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Democratic lawmakers are labeling Elon Musk an "opportunist" after the billionaire denied being "MAGA" last week and shared his regret for putting roughly $450 million toward the GOP in the midterm elections.

"I think that Mr. Musk is an opportunist," Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "I think he's a chameleon. I think he will be whatever benefits him and his business."

"It sounds like buyer's remorse to me," Rep. Christian Menefee, D-Texas, said. "Maybe he should spend his time focusing on his businesses instead of trying to buy politicians."

I SAW THE REAL DOGE FROM THE INSIDE. WHY THE MEDIA GOT DOGE AND ELON ALL WRONG

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk speaks at a rally for former President and Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump at Madison Square Garden in New York, Oct. 27, 2024. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)

The political flip-flop callout comes after Musk made comments distancing himself from President Donald Trump and Republicans on Wednesday during The New York Times' DealBook Summit. Musk has put millions of dollars toward Trump, has previously campaigned with him and worked for the administration.

"Whatever," Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., said when asked about Musk’s comments. "That’s my response. Whatever."

Musk has also been facing wrath from Democratic lawmakers as a potential target of oversight investigations for his time as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

"You're the architect of DOGE," Carter continued. "You wreck people's lives. You tear people's opportunities and their careers apart in a reckless effort to so-called save money when nobody's pocket's been padded with his. If he really wants to do the right thing, demonstrate it, not in word, but in deed."

"I’m certain that he will be the subject of investigations," Rep. Sanford Bishop Jr., D-Ga., said. "We’ll deal with it when we deal with it."

An investigation into Musk and DOGE seems to be at the top of the list for many Democrats as the party pushes for investigations to look into alleged corruption under the Trump administration after the party took back majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.

"I've not seen anything that he's done to reach out to Democrats or help or anything else in that regard," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., said when asked if Democrats would reach out to Musk to work together.

He continued, "What he's done is destroy the State Department [and] destroy diplomacy."

THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS

Elon Musk denied being "MAGA" last week and shared his regret for putting roughly $450 million toward the GOP in the midterm elections. (Getty Images)

Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., urged Democrats to not make oversight investigations the center of their party’s agenda over the next two years with a majority in both the House and the Senate. He said the upcoming years should be focused on "leveraging this majority" to bring results to Americans.

"I think there will obviously be some degree of oversight into what happened with DOGE, and I think rightfully so," Figures said. "But I don't believe that sort of oversight can become the North Star of what the party is all about over the next two years."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who was just elected by his party to serve as speaker of the House, also recently left the door open to potential investigations into Musk when asked by Fox News Digital about the conversations surrounding oversight. He deferred leaving investigation decisions up to Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. — the party’s expected leaders of oversight work.

The Republicans whom Fox News Digital spoke with were not totally convinced that Musk’s recent comments meant he was backing out of supporting Republicans.

"I think Musk is about fiscal responsibility," Rep. Glenn Grothman, R-Wis., said. "And the Republican Party, while it lets you down some of the time, is still the party of fiscal responsibility."

JEFFRIES BRUSHES OFF OPPOSITION FROM FAR-LEFT DEMS WHO VOTED NO: 'WE’RE GOING TO WORK TOGETHER'

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., acknowledged that Republicans in Congress "fell short," excusing the American people for being upset with her party.

"It's totally in his hands, whether he supports [Republicans] or not," Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., said. "But I don't think that there's any question that this Congress fell short, specifically the Senate, and people have a right to be angry. Hell, I'm angry."

Congressional oversight into Musk could come as soon as January, when Democrats officially take control of Congress and leadership of the House Oversight Committee.

Fox News Digital's request for comment from Musk was not immediately returned.

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

One of the top premium cards, the offers many lifestyle-centered benefits and statement credits. Those include several health- and fitness-centered benefits, including an Oura Ring statement credit for up to $200 per calendar year (enrollment is required).

With the end of the calendar year fast approaching, now's a good time to decide whether you can use this credit before it resets.

Here's how this statement credit works and whether it makes sense for you.

One of the many lifestyle statement credits available through the is up to $200 each calendar year toward Oura Ring. Specifically, the statement credit applies to hardware purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. (Enrollment is required.)

The Oura Ring is a wearable, health-tracking smart ring. Some key data it tracks includes:

Imagine an Apple Watch or Fitbit, but in ring form. Oura currently sells the Oura Ring 4 starting at $349 and the newer Oura Ring 5 starting at $399. While this statement credit won't fully cover the cost of a ring, it will get you more than halfway there.

One notable advantage of the Oura Ring is that you don't have to charge it as often as other wearables — the Oura Ring 5 typically lasts six or more days on a full charge.

Related: The best credit cards to maximize fitness spending

Amex states that the statement credit should post within eight weeks, but some TPG staffers have seen it post within days.

If you're trying to use this statement credit before Dec. 31, don't wait for the last minute. Amex relies on the date Oura processes the transaction, which might be a day or two after you place the order.

This is particularly important if you order a sizing kit: The ring itself won't process and ship until you confirm your size in your Oura account. Place your order now to get things started.

Related: Why the new Amex Platinum changes are converting me to a cardmember

This statement credit is a more niche perk that not all cardmembers will be able to use. For starters, many people may prefer other forms of wearables. If health data doesn't interest you, this statement credit won't move the needle either.

Plus, the fact that this statement credit doesn't cover the full cost of the ring may also deter some cardmembers. The out-of-pocket cost will still run you at least $149, unless you land a good sale. You'll also need to pay for an Oura Membership at $5.99 monthly or $69.99 per year.

I hope Amex expands this statement credit to cover a subscription in the future, since it's needed to fully maximize your Oura Ring's features.

Even if Oura Ring is of interest, you may not want to buy a new one every year, meaning some years the benefit may go unused.

If you don't think you’d use the statement credit yourself, you could gift a ring to one of your health- and fitness-minded friends or family members.

It's also important to note that this is a shared statement credit, meaning authorized users do not receive their own.

This sole statement credit shouldn't be the deciding factor on whether you add this card to your wallet, but if you can use it organically, it can help recoup some of the Platinum's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Related: Complete guide to authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card

The Oura Ring statement credit can be valuable for Platinum Card members who already plan to buy a fitness tracker, especially if they can stack it with a sale. However, you might find it smarter to let the statement credit go unused some or all years.

However, it would be ideal if this statement credit were expanded in the future to cover the subscription cost, as this would make it more accessible for more cardmembers to use year after year.
